<margin>+ By the most blessed and most wise Patriarch, Lord John:</margin>

# Number 33.

**Dialectic is the art of arts and the science of sciences, possessing a path toward**
the principles of all methods. And for this reason, it is the first of the sciences.
First, we have Dialectic. This "Dialectic" comes from *dialexis* <note>original: "διαλέξεως" - discourse or debate</note>. And *dialexis* comes from *dialegesthai* <note>original: "διαλέγεσθαι" - to converse or reason</note>. To converse signifies that a part of speech should not be joined together by itself; so that it is the casting forth of one's own intellectual parts. *Dialexis* is also called "discursive thought" <note>original: "διανοητική"</note>; it is clear to all and has been spoken of similarly by those to whom the parts of speech belong. But Dialectic does not consist without implanted speech <note>original: "λόγου" - Logos can mean word, speech, or reason</note>, nor is speech implanted without the intellectual <unclear>light</unclear>. Sensible things, however, are sound; a noise is made at night or otherwise as it is able to be produced in the breath. It is also said properly that hearing is the cutting back of the visual powers <note>The text here reflects ancient theories of perception where senses interact or compete</note>, for the spirit of the air is set before it. Voice is a sound, specifically the voice of an ensouled being. But [mere noise] is not voice. Even ensouled things produce the "noise" of the animal and the beast, as it is called. It is shaped by the natural organs. The natural organs by which the voice is shaped are said to be these: the lips, the teeth, the tongue, the palate, the larynx, and the pharynx. The characteristic of intellectual voice is that it surpasses that of inanimate bodies, such as the striking of strings. That which is articulated <note>original: "περιφθέγχτιστος"</note> is that which produces similar [sounds]. <margin>signification</margin> **Every voice is both sensible and significant. And this**
significant voice is like that of the <unclear>animal</unclear> <unclear>and</unclear>. Because it is not prior, nor is it the cause. For example: "Man." The implanted hearing is also significant as its own property. For example, the lowing of an ox...
**Every significant voice is a sensible and significant voice. And this**
voice is significant of a sound, so that all [is included]. The same applies to the animal. Just as every significant [sound] of irrational creatures is significant, so too in the case of spirits it is to be in a form of desire. **A voice is not significant which is that which is not**
placed by the tongue to be heard from the animal. For example: "Man" <note>The author is distinguishing between natural sounds and conventional language</note>. All significant voice is implanted, but speech <note>Logos</note> does not consist of names alone. For example, the Name and the Verb. It is not significant by convention except with [other parts]. For example, a sentence. <margin>signification<br/>definition<br/>of the name</margin> **A name is a voice**
significant by convention, without time, of which no part is significant in isolation, but only as an utterance. Significant voice falls upon that which is defined, as do the law and the case <note>original: "πτῶσις" - in grammar, this refers to noun declensions/inflections</note>. The differences of the utterance and of the whole are pronounced significantly. Regarding that which is by convention, these are the differences of nature.

# Page 500
## No 33

† <unclear>Book</unclear> of <unclear>Dialectic</unclear> by the same father, John <note>original: "Ιωανου" - referring to St. John of Damascus, a 7th-8th century theologian and philosopher</note>:

**D**ialectic is the art of arts and the science of sciences, possessing a path toward the principles of all methods. And for this reason, it appropriately encounters the student of dialectic first among the sciences. It is called "dialectic" from "dialexis" <note>discourse or conversation</note>. This comes from "dialegesthai" <note>to converse</note>, which signifies speaking with someone. It means to speak a word with reasoning <note>syllogism</note>, involving both the one putting forward the argument and the one responding. Or it comes from "dialegesthai" and "diakrinesthai" <note>to distinguish or discern</note>, according to which the ancients and those engaging in dialogue make divisions. 

But since dialectic cannot be practiced without the use of speech <note>logos</note>, nor can speech be used without the use of the voice, and every voice is a sound <note>psophos</note>, which hearing primarily perceives. It is said "primarily" because it also strikes the air or because sounds are heard within. For it holds a similar quality through the sound. **Of** sounds, some are voices, and others are not voices. A voice is a sound of a living body, shaped by the natural organs. The natural organs by which the voice is shaped are called the lips, teeth, tongue, palate, larynx, and pharynx. That which is not called a voice is the sound produced from the collision of inanimate bodies, such as the breaking of wood, or the clap of thunder, or similar things. <margin>and these</margin> **Of** all voices, some are significant <note>meaningful</note>, and others are non-significant. A significant voice is one which we have established by convention <note>thesis</note> to <unclear>call</unclear> things, such as "man." A non-significant voice is one that reveals none of the things that exist, such as "blituri" <note>a traditional nonsense word used by ancient logicians, similar to "gibberish"</note>.

**Of** all significant voices, some are significant by nature, and others... a voice significant by nature is that which <unclear>shows</unclear> the same things to all people; for example, the <unclear>groan</unclear> of those who are ill is significant. And the voice of the species of birds, such as quails. **A** voice significant by convention is that which <unclear>submits</unclear> to those who establish it according to the will of those establishing it, such as "man." **Of** all significant voices by convention, some are simple and uncompounded, such as the noun <note>onoma</note> and the verb <note>rhema</note>. Others are composite and compounded, such as a sentence <note>logos</note>. <margin>establishing / signifies</margin> **A** noun is a significant voice by convention, without time, of which no part signifies anything separately from the whole. The word "voice" is placed in the definition as the genus of the noun. The word "significant" is added to differentiate it from a non-significant voice. The phrase "by convention" <gloss>established for all</gloss> is added to differentiate it from a voice significant by nature.

...a significant sound. The phrase **"apart from time"** <note>original: "ἐκ χρόνου"</note> serves to distinguish it from the verb, which signifies time. The phrase "not even a part" and the rest serves to distinguish it from the sentence <note>original: "λόγος" (logos), here meaning a complete statement or phrase</note>, whose parts signify something when separated. The term **"definite"** <note>original: "ὡρισμένον"</note> distinguishes it from the "indefinite noun," such as "not-man" <note>The text uses "man" (anthropos) as the example of a definite noun</note>, which the older thinkers <note>likely referring to the Pre-Socratics or early Academics</note> used to <unclear>call</unclear> a proper noun, but it is actually an indefinite noun. The phrase "or of cases" distinguishes the oblique cases of nouns from the nominative case, and likewise for others; these were called nouns by the older thinkers, but they are actually "cases" of nouns. Only the nominative form is properly <margin>concerning the verb</margin> a noun.

A **verb** <note>original: "ῥῆμα" (rhema)</note> is a significant sound, by convention, including the notion of time, of which no part signifies anything when separated. The **"definite"** parts themselves, being with time, are the **difference** from the noun, which signifies without time. The term **"definite"** distinguishes it from the "indefinite verb," such as "he is not healthy" <note>original: "οὐχ ὑγιαίνει"</note>. These were considered verbs by the older thinkers, but they are indefinite verbs. The "being" <note>referring to the present tense</note> is used to distinguish it from the oblique tenses of verbs, such as "he was healthy" or **"they two ran"** <note>original: "ἐδραμότην" (dual form)</note> and similar forms, because those are not called verbs, but "cases" <note>inflections</note> of a verb. For according to some, only the verb in the present tense and the direct case is named a verb. All the rest are said to be oblique verbs for the same reason. All other distinctions apply to verbs in the same way as they do to nouns. Just as the word "dialectic" would be a **noun** in the strict sense of the word.

What remains are the noun and the verb. The other parts of the <margin>concerning the sentence</margin> category are **likewise** significant. A **sentence** <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> is a significant sound by convention, of which some of the parts signify something by themselves when separated. The phrase "by convention" and the rest are placed here to differentiate it from the noun and the verb, whose parts signify nothing when separated. All other attributes are credited to the sentence itself, just as they were to the noun and the verb.

Of sentences, some are "declarative" <note>original: "ἀποφαντικοί"</note> and others are "incomplete." Those are declarative which, by voicing the whole thought, provide a full answer to everyone, such as "a man runs." Incomplete sentences are those that do not reveal the whole mind <unclear>upon</unclear> the <unclear>thought</unclear> <unclear>value</unclear>, such as "a white man." Of complete sentences, some are "definitive," such as "a man runs"; others are "propositional," such as "every [man] is true"; others are "vocative" <note>or optative/prayerful</note>, such as "may he be a good heir"; and others are "hypothetical," such as "if he is a man, he is an animal." Of all these, the definitive...

Generally, there are three types of matter: necessary, contingent, and impossible. <note>In logic, "matter" refers to the inherent relationship between the subject and the predicate.</note>
The **necessary** is that in which the <term>predicate</term> <note>The part of the sentence that makes an assertion about the subject.</note> always belongs to the <term>subject</term>. <note>The person or thing the sentence is about.</note>
For example: "Man is an animal"; it is a necessity that man is an animal. The **contingent**
is that in which the predicate is able to both belong and not belong to the subject.
<note>The scribe appears to have slightly confused the terms here, as the following examples of "white man" and "black raven" are standard examples of contingent or inseparable accidents.</note>
Necessary things are those [whose absence] brings destruction to the subject. For example: "The man is white"; and "The raven is
black." The **impossible** is that in which the predicate cannot belong
to the subject; for example: "Man is a donkey." It is necessary to know that in **necessary matter**,
the affirmations are true and the negations are false; but not the reverse.
However, it is not the case that both are false in **contingent matter**; for example: "Every
man is white"; "No man is white." If one says the reverse, "Every man
is healthy," it is false; "Every man is healthy"; and the reverse. For example: "Every
man is healthy"; "No man is healthy." And likewise for particular [propositions]; for example: "Some
man is healthy"; "No man is white." And in contingent matter, when the
predicate is an inseparable <term>accident</term>, <note>A quality that isn't part of the essential definition but is always present, like "blackness" in a raven.</note> both cannot be
false at the same time. It is necessary to know that in **impossible matter**, the affirmations are false, while
the negations are true. And not the reverse. However, it is not the case that both are
true in contingent matter; generally, when the law [of propositions] relates to one another in these
matters, it follows the law of contraries. The law of contradictories is that one must be true.
Where the particular negative [is true], the universal is false. And the reverse. For in no
matter can both be true; nor can both be false at the same time. <insert>Laws</insert>
Regarding subalterns: when the universal is true, the particular is also
true; but not the reverse. For it does not follow that if the particular is true, the universal
is true; and the reverse. And if the particular is false,
the universal is false; but not the reverse. Regarding propositions
which have both terms reversed in their order: this is
**conversion**, which can be simple, or by accident, or by contraposition.
Again, conversion is the process of making the subject become the predicate,
while maintaining the same quality and quantity. Let us look at the method...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical propositions, specifically focusing on the rules of conversion (antistrophe) and the structure of hypothetical and complex statements.</meta>

The universal negative <term>universal negative: a statement of the form 'No A is B'</term> converts into a universal negative; for example, "No human is a stone," and likewise, "No stone is a human." And conversely for a living being: if "Every human is a living being." There is also conversion by accident <term>conversion by accident: changing the quantity of a proposition (e.g., universal to particular) during conversion</term> when the subject becomes the predicate and vice versa, while the quality remains the same but the quantity is altered.

In this way, the universal affirmative converts into the particular affirmative; and the universal negative into the particular negative. For example, "Every human is a living being," then "Some living being is a human." Conversion by opposition <note>original: "κατὰ ἀντίθεσιν ἀντιστροφή"</note> is to speak of the predicate from the subject and vice versa, while the quality and quantity remain the same, but the defining terms are changed. If you define it so, the universal affirmative does not convert into the particular negative. For example, "Every human is a living being"; "Everything that is not a living being is not a human." It is the same as "Every human is like a stone"; therefore, not every stone <insert>for</insert> is a human; and "A human is not a stone"; and "That which is not a stone is not a human." It should be noted that in the premises, when the subject is about to be written, whatever it may be, the "color" <note>likely referring to the logical 'form' or 'character'</note> also happens in the predicate.

And after these things, the whole is applied to the underlying subject. Thus, conversion by contradiction is the movement from a particular or indefinite statement to a universal proposition. We might also speak then about the hypothetical proposition; for a hypothetical proposition is one that is categorical through the use of connecting particles. The hypothetical proposition is chosen by the sound of the phrase <note>The Greek text here is slightly corrupted or uses obscure grammatical jargon regarding "the sound of the branch"</note> according to the well-placed position, such as "being" and "the same" converting. In all universal propositions, there are parts of a sequence. The copulative <term>copulative: a 'both/and' statement</term> must be understood: while hypothetical statements are sequences in the connection of causal predicates, they follow along. For example, "If Socrates runs, Socrates moves." Of these, the categorical part is said to immediately entail "being," as the wise say; and when one says: "nor again the things being forced." A copulative statement exists in the connection of causal predicates, as when one says: "Socrates reads and Plato discourses." A disjunctive <term>disjunctive: an 'either/or' statement</term> statement exists in the connection of causal predicates, not in the conjunction; for example, "Socrates runs or Plato discourses." Regarding the conversion of the sequence of hypotheticals, it is investigated. The antecedent and the consequent must be true from the converting term; for example, "If someone has died, he does not live, he is not"; which every reciprocal sequence is true and necessary. We have already spoken of certain things...

as to know. Furthermore, its falsehood [is known] from the impossible recovery of the premises without the application <note>The author is discussing how a logical premise fails if its components cannot be reconciled</note>. For example: "God is strongest as he is sweetest." Furthermore, regarding interwoven statements <term>interwoven: Greek *sympeplegmenon*, referring to complex or compound propositions</term>, truth is sought in the fact that all of their parts are true. For example: "Man is an animal, and he walks." Furthermore, falsehood [is found] at the beginning; for being somewhere, I suppose, negates its being false. For example: "Man is an animal" and "A horse is a stone." Furthermore, [one seeks] truth in the hypothetical from the recovery of its true part. For example: "Man is an animal" or "A horse is a stone." As many as were placed without the second [part] resulted in the negation of its parts. But they are invalid. For example: "Man is an animal"; for in this way [it is] as a coloring agent. Furthermore, its falsehood is found in seeking whether both its parts are false-born. For example: "Man is a donkey" and "A horse is a stone." Consequently, we shall consider the propositions that are brought together as equals; these are the ones contrary to the common [rules] for this reason. If the negative particle is added to any universal affirmative interwoven statement, it is equivalent to the alternative negative. For example: "Not every man runs" or "He does not run away."

<margin>Another rule</margin> If the negative particle is added to any universal negative interwoven statement, it is equivalent to the alternative affirmative. For example: "Every man is not an animal." He himself is of the essence as an animal. It belongs to no man. "Every man runs." <margin>¶</margin> ### The Universal Categorical: The Highest Genus **Concerning the Five Voices.** <note>The "Five Voices" or "Quinque Voces" refer to the five predicables: Genus, Species, Difference, Property, and Accident.</note>

In the strict sense, only that which is said of many things is called "categorical." This is understood in a general way. Either it is called categorical in that sense alone, or insofar as it is predicated of many. That which is taken as categorical in the strict sense is the same as the <term>universal</term> <note>original: "katholou"</note>. It differs from it only in name. For the "categorical" is defined by its complete designation, while the "universal" is defined by its being. Thus, the categorical is that which is by nature predicated of many; the universal is that which is naturally suited to be over many. The categorical, indivisible universal is signified in five ways: **Genus, Difference, Species, Property, and Accident.** Hence, we shall examine these matters here. <insert>**Concerning Genus.**</insert> <insert>**From where the term Genus is derived.**</insert> For it is said to be a collection of certain many things who have a relationship to one another according to a single origin. For example, a collection of those who belong to the same lineage, because the "genus" <note>In this context, "genus" also means "family" or "race"</note> descends from one person. In a transitional sense, it is like the origin of the birth of that land—for example, those associated with Aphrodite <note>original: "Kypris," an epithet for Aphrodite</note>. In a general sense, all things that are offspring and experiences and the "genus" itself are spoken of here.

For example, "animal" is predicated of "man" and of "horse." These differ in the "What is it?" <note>meaning their essential nature is different</note>. Regarding the other point, it considers that which differs in species; for it is not enough to say "whatever is said of many," since those things said of the same thing are not called genera. 

Now, "the same" is used in <gloss>three ways</gloss>: for something is the same. It can be the same in **number**. Things are the same in number when they have many names but the object itself is one. For example, "cloak" and "mantle" <note>original: "λώπιον καὶ ἱμάτιον" - two Greek words for the same garment</note>. These are also the same in species, and the species is the same. For example, Socrates and Plato in relation to "man." 

Things that are the same in number are spoken of in three ways: either by **name**, or by **definition**, or by **property**, or by **accident**. 
*   They are called the same by **name** when the object is one, but the names are many, such as "Marcus" and "Tullius" <note>referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>. 
*   They are the same by **definition** when one is the definition and the other is the <margin>name</margin>, such as "rational mortal animal" and "man." 
*   They are called the same by **property** when one is the property and the other is the subject, such as "man" and "that which is capable of laughter." 
*   They are the same by **accident** when one is an accident and the other is the subject, such as "Socrates" and "the one sitting in the Lyceum." 

In the same way, we speak of "differing." Things differ in number when they are distinct individuals. Those called "differing" in the following sense are those of different genera, such as the subjects: for example, Socrates and Ballias <note>a common textbook name in ancient logic</note>. For Socrates is a man, but Ballias is a horse. Things differ in number when "man" <gloss>and</gloss> is not different in number; for example, Socrates and Plato. 

For the **species** is also said in the "What is it?" so as to be given similarly in response to a <unclear>greater</unclear> or developing question. For example, "animal" is said, and as a genus, so also "man" is given to those asking "What is it?" For "animal" is predicated of man in the "What is it?" 

We also define the species otherwise in this way: a genus is that which is constitutive of the species. The species is divided into the **most general genus** and the <gloss>as it were</gloss> **intermediate** <gloss>and</gloss> **species**. The <gloss>the</gloss> most general genus is the genus above which there is no <unclear>higher</unclear> genus. And again, the **most specific** species is the species which is not <unclear>again</unclear> a species <note>meaning it cannot be divided into further sub-species, only individuals</note>. And similarly it is likely. And indeed these are: **Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Action, Passion, Position, Time, Place, State.** These ten are called the "most general genera" because there is no genus beyond these. For "Being" <note>original: "τὸ ὄν"</note> is said of all <gloss>ten</gloss> genera equivocally <note>meaning the word "being" has different meanings for each category</note> in many ways; it is not said univocally.

# Difference is spoken of in three ways: commonly, specially, and most specially. A common difference
is that by which one thing differs from another by any <term>otherness</term> <note>original: "heterotes"</note> or even by a separable accident of the thing itself. For example,
insofar as Socrates sitting differs from Plato standing. Or even from himself <note>e.g., Socrates sitting vs. Socrates standing</note>. A special
difference is that which occurs through an inseparable but always present accident.
For example, being black-eyed, or grey-eyed, or hook-nosed. These are inseparable accidents because <insert>the</insert>
they are always present. The most special difference is that which occurs through a certain essential, self-sufficient
constitutive difference. Just as man <note>Abbreviation for anthropos</note> differs from horses by being rational. And
it is placed in the final position, and this difference is analyzed. They define
it thus: **Difference** is that which is predicated of many things that differ in species in the
"of what quality" <note>The category of "quale" or "poion ti"</note>. For example, "rational" is predicated of man and
of others that differ in species. For we men are rational,
as Porphyry intends. But the inclusion of "mortal" does not in any way
separate it <note>the essence</note>. For it is predicated above it, in the "of what quality it is," which
we would not answer in response to a question of "what is it?" but rather "of what quality is it?"
When asked "of what quality is a thing?" we say "man,"
we would not answer "rational" <note>to the question "what is it?"</note>. For **in** the way "rational" is predicated
of man, it is in the "of what quality it is." They **define** difference in another way as well:
the presence of that which makes the species. For example, man [as a species] of animal. These are the logical
types of difference. **It must be known** that difference is itself also a genus
and in a way divisive, but in different manners. For it is constitutive of the
species but divisive of the genus. For example, "rational" divides "animal"
along with its opposite difference. For we say that of animals,
some are rational, others are irrational. These same differences are also
constitutive of the animal's difference. For every difference and every specific form
constitutes the species. **In** its constitutive role, that of man belongs to him.
Just as "mortal" is contained by some, or by animals, but is constitutive of
man. **It must be known** that Boethius <note>original: "Boulios," likely referring to the commentator Boethius</note> says only the species is defined.
For a definition consists of the genus and the constitutive [differences] or the differences themselves.
And only the species possesses both genus and differences.

### Concerning the Property. The property is divided in three ways, or is spoken of in three ways. For it is said...

A property is "unique" in one sense when it belongs to some individuals but not to all; for example, practicing geometry or medicine in a human being. For these belong to some humans and not to all. In another sense, it is unique when it belongs to all but not to only one species; for example, being two-footed belongs to every human, but not only to humans <note>original: "δίποδι" (dipodi). The author notes that while all humans are bipeds, other creatures like birds are as well, so it is not "unique" to humanity alone.</note>. In a third sense, it is unique when it belongs to all and only to one species, but not always; for example, turning grey belongs to all humans and only to humans, but not always <note>i.e., only in old age</note>; likewise with growing old.

In the fourth sense, it is "unique" in the strict sense: that which belongs to only one species, to all members of it, and always. For example, the capacity for laughter <term>the risible: the natural ability to laugh, often used in logic as the classic example of a unique human property</term> in relation to the human being. For if one is a human, one has the capacity for laughter. For this is the "unique property" and the truly unique one which applies to the whole species, converting <note>original: "ἀντιστρέφων" (antistrephon). In logic, "converting" means the subject and predicate can be swapped: "All humans are capable of laughter" and "All beings capable of laughter are humans."</note> with the nature of the human. It is in this sense that "unique property" is spoken of in the five categories <note>referring to the five "predicables" of Porphyry: genus, species, difference, property, and accident</note>; for thus he set it forth.

A unique property belongs to only one and to all, and in this way they convert with the things themselves; yet it does not signify the "essence" <term>essence: literally "the what it was to be," the core definition of a thing</term> of the thing. For example, the capacity for laughter in a human. The phrase "not signifying the essence" is added in the description of the unique property <insert>or the accident</insert> to distinguish it from the definition. For the definition is also predicated convertibly of the whole thing, but it *does* signify the essence of the thing. For example: "a rational, mortal, sensitive animal." This converts with the unique property <note>meaning it covers the same group of beings</note> and reveals the essence. Therefore, every definition is made through essential characteristics. For everything higher is convertible with that which is lower than itself. For definition is defined thus: a definition is a statement signifying the essence.

**The unique property does not signify the essence; or the accident**

An accident is that which can be present or absent without the destruction of the subject; for example, whiteness, blackness, or the act of sitting. For these can be present in the same subject and be absent from it without the destruction of the subject <note>A person remains a person whether they are sitting or standing, or if their hair turns from black to white.</note>. It is also defined this way: an accident is that which is neither a genus, nor a species, nor a difference, nor a unique property, yet it exists in the thing. And these are as follows: an accident is that which is capable of being present and not being present in the same thing; for example, whiteness or sitting in a human. Of these last two descriptions, the second is better; since regarding the first four, it is necessary to happen to know what a genus, species, difference, or unique property is. But if one defines their unique characteristics by themselves, we grasp the truth concerning those things we know in their own right.

<summary>This page explains the logical distinction between "unique properties" (propria) and "accidents," using the classic Porphyrian framework to define what makes a human being unique (the capacity for laughter) versus what is merely incidental (sitting or color).</summary>
<keywords>unique property, accident, definition, essence, risibility, Porphyry, Isagoge, logic, Aristotle</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the logical analysis of Porphyry’s Isagoge (Introduction to Aristotle's Categories), specifically focusing on the "Five Universals": genus, species, difference, property, and accident.</meta>

Of **accidents** <note>term: accident (symbebekos). A non-essential quality that can change without the subject losing its identity, such as being seated or having a tan.</note>, one kind is **separable**, such as whiteness or the act of sleeping in a human. The other kind is **inseparable**, such as the blackness in a crow or an Ethiopian, and the whiteness in a swan. While blackness is an accident for the crow, these cannot be removed or even conceived of as absent <insert>not</insert> without the destruction of the underlying subject. Therefore, **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), whose "Isagoge" became the standard textbook on logic in the Middle Ages.</note> says that they cannot be "undone," for a crow cannot be thought of as white, nor an Ethiopian as white, without the destruction of the subject.

Accidents are further divided: one kind is **common**, and the other is **proper** <note>term: proper (idion). A quality that belongs only to one species, like "the ability to laugh" for humans.</note>. A common accident is like whiteness or blackness in general. A proper accident is like the specific whiteness of **Socrates** or the snub-nosedness of **Plato**.

**Genus** <note>term: genus (genos). A broad category, like "Animal."</note> is predicated of all those things in the categories that are present. However, the **species** <note>term: species (eidos). A specific sub-category, like "Human."</note> differ. The genus differs from the others by being predicated of more things than the others. The **difference** <note>term: difference (diaphora). The specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus, like "rationality."</note> differs from the genus in that it is predicated in the "of what kind" <note>original: "en to poion"</note>, whereas the genus is predicated in the "what it is" <note>original: "en to ti"</note>. Or, the difference is not an accident of the genus, but it differs from other differences by being predicated of many things that differ in species.

**Property** and **genus** also differ. The **accident** differs from these because accidents admit of "intensity and relaxation" <note>term: intensity and relaxation (epitasis and anesis). The logical concept that qualities like "heat" or "whiteness" can be more or less intense, whereas essential definitions cannot.</note>. But the difference, being perceived, does not admit of the "more and the less."

The **species** differs from the **genus** because the genus contains all the species, but the species does not contain the genus. The species differs from the **difference** because the difference <insert>not</insert> is more extensive but becomes part of the definition, as in "rational" and "human." The species, if it contains another species, is sufficient; but the genus does not exist as another thing except as a potentiality within the genus.

The species differs from the **property** because the species is prior by nature to the property, while the property is posterior <note>i.e., the definition of "Human" must exist before the property of "being able to laugh" can be attributed to it.</note>. For definitions are differences and they increase, but these are similar differences.

The species differs from the **accident** because the species is predicated in the "what it is," while the accident is in the "of what kind" or "how it is." And the species contains the accident, for every accident by its nature is always in a specific subject.

The **property** differs from the **accident** because the property is predicated of only one [species], while the accident is predicated of many. The accident is first in individuals, and later in genera and species. For "human" and "animal" do not have their being except through the existence of **Socrates** and **Plato**. The property belongs first—

<summary>This page provides a technical breakdown of the "Five Universals" in Aristotelian logic, explaining how genus, species, difference, property, and accident are distinguished from one another.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Aristotle, Logic, Genus, Species, Accident, Socrates, Plato, Predication, Five Universals</keywords>

--- Page 30 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical definitions, specifically focusing on the relationship between the "five universals" (genus, species, difference, property, and accident) and the way terms are predicated of subjects, leading into Aristotle's Categories.</meta>

As for the species, all these things apply to individuals. The difference, the species, and the property <note>These are three of the five "predicables" or ways a thing can be described in logic.</note> apply to the genus in cases where they are shared by all things of which they might be predicated. However, the **accident** <note>A non-essential quality, like being "seated" or "tan."</note> is not shared by all. Furthermore, the genus, the difference, the species, and the property are predicated **synonymously** <note>original: "συνωνύμως" (synonymously). In Aristotelian logic, this means the name and the definition both apply to the subject.</note>. But the accident is not predicated synonymously, but **heteronymously** <note>Under a different name or definition.</note>.

To be predicated synonymously is to be predicated of something where the name and the definition are one and the same. For example, "man" and the individual name are predicated of Socrates and Plato. For instance, "Socrates is a man." All these are predicated according to the same definition. For example, "Socrates is a living being, rational and mortal" <note>This is the classic definition of a human being in ancient philosophy.</note>. It is the same for other stable things; this is also how being defined works. Therefore, the universal name is predicated of all things beneath it, and not only according to the definition. That which is the specific definition is predicated both of the thing itself and its attributes.

That which is predicated of things now is the "distinction." And thus it is predicated even with different definitions. From these, it will not shine forth synonymously, but rather **homonymously** or **paronymously**. To be predicated homonymously is to be predicated by name but with different definitions, while the name itself remains unchanged. For example, the word "dog" <note>original: "κύων" (kuon). A famous example in logic: it can mean a barking land animal, a sea-dog (shark/seal), or the Dog Star (Sirius).</note> is predicated by name of the land animal, the sea creature, and the celestial cause. The definitions of all these differ, even though they appear under the same name.

**Paronyms** <note>Words derived from another with a change in termination.</note> are those called after something by a change in the case or inflection of the difference, while the name retains the same designation. For example, from "grammar" comes the "grammarian"; from "bravery," the "brave"; and from "whiteness," the "white." These names are said to be predicated paronymously. Yet, in another sense, the accident is sometimes said to be predicated synonymously.

## On the Ten Categories

<margin>P</margin> First, it is necessary to know the essentials of the categories and the things that must be grasped beforehand, so that we may proceed in every respect. **Homonyms** are those of which only the name is common, but the definition of the essence corresponding to the name is different. For example, "animal" <note>original: "ζῶον" (zoon), which can mean both a "living being" and a "figure/image" in a painting.</note> applies to both a painted man and a real one, and even to a drawing. Only the name is common to them, but the definition according to the name is different. **Synonyms** are <unclear>called</unclear> those of which the name...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical definitions, likely following an introduction to Aristotelian categories. The text focuses on the relationship between names and definitions, the classification of speech, and the various ways one thing can be said to be "in" another.</meta>

A common term <note>original: "κοινόν" (koinon) - referring here to synonyms or univocal terms</note> is one where the definition of the essence <note>original: "λόγος τῆς οὐσίας" (logos tēs ousias)</note> is the same according to the name. For example, the name "animal" is common to its specific types; both the definition and the name are said to be the same. A human is an animal. A horse is a sensitive animal <note>meaning an animal possessing sensation</note>. An ox is an animated, sensitive animal. This name is common to them, and their definition according to the name is the same. For one must not define a human according to the name without indicating "animated and sensitive." And the ox likewise. **Paronyms** <note>original: "παρώνυμα" - derivatives</note> are those things which get their designation from something else, differing only in the case-ending of the name; for example, "the grammarian" from "grammar." **Of words** that are spoken, some are complex <note>original: "συμπλεπλεγμένα" (sympeplegmena) - combined into a sentence</note>, such as "a man runs"; others are without complexity <note>simple terms</note>, such as "man," "stone," or "runs."

But before the whole or the part of the essence of each thing is rendered, it is not spoken of according to the nine senses of "being in something" <note>original: "ἐν τίνι εἶναι" (en tini einai) - a classic Aristotelian inquiry into the relationship of containment or inherence</note>. This will be necessary for the underlying division, since it happens that these inquiries are divided thus:

**First**, something is said to be in another as a part is in the whole, or in the whole. For example, the finger in the hand, and the wall in the house. In a **second** way, it is said as the whole is in its own parts, such as the house in the walls, or [the body] in the hands—though not as a part. In a **third** way, "being in something" is said as the species <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos)</note> is in the genus <note>original: "γένος" (genos)</note>. For example, man is in "animal," and horse is in "animal," and other things are in their genus. In a **fourth** way, as the genus is in the species; or to put it simply, as the definition is in the thing being defined. In a **fifth** way, "being in something" is said as the form is in the matter; for example, a shape <note>original: "τύχη" (tyche), likely a scribal error for "τύπος" (typos) or "σχήμα" (schema) meaning form/shape</note> in the body, and whiteness in the wall. This fifth way is divided: either into those things which are essential, such as the soul of the human, or those which are accidental <note>original: "συμβεβηκότα" (symbebēkota)</note>, such as whiteness in the human. These first ones are properly said to be "in something" as the form is in the matter. The rest are said to be in something as accidents in a subject <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon)</note>, such as whiteness in the wall and grammar in the body. In a **sixth** way, "being in something" is said as being in the power of an agent, such as affairs being in the hands of the ruler. In a **seventh** way, it is said as being in the end <note>the goal or purpose</note>, such as virtue being in happiness. In an **eighth** way, it is said as being in a vessel; and simply put, in a place, such as wine in the jar. **Of beings**, some are said of a subject, but are in no subject; for example, "man" as a species, and the specific differences.

All things are said to be substance <note>original: "ousia" — the fundamental reality or essence of a thing</note>, but this is the name of substance; for example, man <note>Abbreviation for man (anthropos)</note> is a rational animal. Of beings, some are said of a certain subject <note>original: "hypokeimenon" — that which lies beneath; the underlying thing being discussed</note> but are in no subject to be predicated; for example, "animal" is said of "man." But "man" is also said of each individual. And color and whiteness [are similarly distinguished]. To be "in a subject" means to exist in something not as a part, but as something that cannot exist separately from that in which it is; for example, whiteness in a wall. Others are neither said of a subject nor are in a subject; for example, a particular man. These are indicative of all individuals. Others are said of a subject and are in a certain subject; for example, the genera and the species of other things are said to be and are predicated of all those things under them. And if they are species of something, they exist as accidents <note>original: "symbebekos" — a non-essential property or attribute</note> in the subject. And of no subject [are some things said], such as the color whiteness and that of whiteness and of blackness, which are in the body and in the subject.

And some things are in the subject and are said of no subject; for example, the immortality of quality, as it is in the soul in the body. To these, it is an accident in a subject; and it is not said of either subject. This same color is in the subject—that is, the body—which is not said of any other subject; for some of the colors are said to be [in things]. But when opposites occur, or those things which are, that which is said of the predicate, the accident of the subject will be stated; for example, man is an animal; so that man is an animal; so that each individual is also an animal. Of things that differ and are not subaltern to one another <note>i.e., not ranked one under the other in a hierarchy</note>, the differences are in species, and the differences [are distinct]; for example, "animal" and "knowledge" have different differences. For the differences of "animal" are "mortal" and "immortal"; for beings are divided, as for example, of animals some are rational and some are irrational. But the differences of knowledge are "physical," "ethical," and "logical"; for the sciences are divided by these differences. For example, of the species, one is physical, another ethical, and another logical. Of things said according to a single combination, each is either a substance or an accident; as the accident is either quantity, or quality, or relation, or place, or time, or reference, or place, or time, or posture, or state, or action, or passion. Substance is, to speak in outline, for example, "man."

<margin>Concerning Substance</margin>
**F**ollowing these, we must speak concerning the categories of being; and first, concerning **Substance** <note>original: "ousia," meaning the fundamental essence or "thingness" of an object</note>. This is the category that most distinguishes itself from the others. Substance is divided into **Primary** and **Secondary**. Primary substance is that which is called so in the most proper, basic, and strictest sense: it is neither said of a subject nor is it in a subject. For example, "this specific man" or "this specific horse." Secondary substances are the **Species** <note>original: "eide"</note> in which the primary substances exist, and the **Genera** <note>original: "gene," the broader classifications</note> of those species. For example, "man" is the species, and "animal" is the genus. For just as the specific man exists within the species "man," so too the species "man" exists within the genus "animal."

These also share in the definition of each type of substance. For this reason, they primarily underlie other things. The genera and species are called secondary substances because they are secondarily in a subject compared to other things. For example, a man is called "literate" or "white," yet he is also a substance. In cases where something is predicated of a subject, both the name and the definition are predicated. For example, "man" is predicated of the <unclear>individual</unclear>. Of all subjects, if there are many, the name is predicated but not necessarily the definition of the subject. For example, "white"; this thing is white. In some cases, nothing prevents the name from being predicated of the subject while the definition cannot be. For example, "white" is said of a subject, but the definition of "white" is never predicated of the subject <note>The author is distinguishing between an accidental quality like "whiteness" and the essential definition of the object itself</note>.

Primary substances are more truly substances than species and genera. Because the species underlies the primary substance in a proper sense. For just as the genus will underlie, so too will the species. And the species underlies more properly, just as the same things have experienced the same. But the species are the most specific of substances, such as "man" and similar things. **H**aving observed these points, we must speak concerning the common characteristics of substance. It is common to every substance not to be in a subject; for being "in a subject" belongs only to **Accidents** <note>original: "symbebekotos," non-essential properties like color or size</note>; and this is demonstrated also in the case of primary substances...

And the things of the <unclear>difference</unclear> also fit this. <insert>Furthermore</insert>, it is a property of substance that, while remaining the same through change, it is able to admit contraries. For example, the same man is at one time white and at another time black.

### On Quantity.

Of quantity, one kind is continuous, and the other is discrete <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted as individual units, like people or coins.</note>.

is a multitude of units as if joined together. Similarly, in speech, the

### Concerning Relatives

<margin>Concerning Relatives</margin> Things are called "relatives" <note>original: "πρός τι" - literally "toward something"</note> when they are said to be what they are of other things, or are related to something else in any other way. For example, the "double" is called the double of a half, and the "half" is the half of a double. Also, the "greater" is the greater of the less, and the "similar" is similar to the similar. There are three properties of these relative terms. The first is that they use a single reference. For example, they are called by the same names because of the same cause, just as the "similar" is called similar to the similar, and the "equal" is equal to the equal. The second is according to the relation, such as a "master" is a master of a master <note>The text here seems to struggle with the reciprocal nature of the master-slave relationship</note>. The third is according to their existence <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>. For example, a "slave" is called the slave of a master. Therefore, by a reciprocal exchange, they belong to one another. These and others are of this kind: the master was the master of a slave, and the father of a son, and the double of the half; and the slave is called the slave of a master, and the son of a father, and the half by the double. After these things, let us speak of the common properties of relatives. The first property is that contrariety exists among relatives. For example, virtue is the contrary of vice. But this is not true of all relatives; for the "double" has no contrary among relatives. For there is nothing contrary to the double, nor to the triple. The second property is that they admit of "more" and "less." For example, the "similar" is called more or less similar, and likewise the "dissimilar." But this does not apply to all relatives. For the "double" is not called more or less double, nor is the "triple," nor is the "greater" called more or less greater. The third property of relatives is that they are spoken of in terms of reciprocity <note>original: "ἀντιστρέφοντα" - turning back or converting</note>.

For example, a father is a father of a son; and from these, this also follows. And the "double" does not exist apart from this, just as the double is double of its half. For they say that these **relatives** <note>original: "ἀναφορικά" (anaphorika), here referring to terms that exist in relation to something else</note> are **simultaneous by nature**. For father and son, and double and half, coexist simultaneously by nature. The most significant characteristic is that relatives **convert equally**; for example, the double is the double of a half; and if the half exists, the double also exists. And there is yet another definition of relatives: relatives are those things for which their very being is the same as being related to something in some way. This is the specific definition of relatives. For it is characteristic of relatives to convert equally. Regarding relatives, even that which is not defined is defined; for example, when specific doubles are formed, it is not a double in a defined way; just as the sun, conversely, is among those things where the predicates can be taken to infinity.

-><margin>Concerning Quality</margin><-

<insert>Quality is that according to which we are said to be "of a certain sort,"</insert> just as people are called "white" according to their whiteness. This category also has its own features (just like relatives). There are **four kinds of quality**. The first is **disposition** <note>original: "διάθεσις" (diathesis), a temporary state</note> and **habit** <note>original: "ἕξις" (hexis), a stable or permanent state</note>. A habit is more noble because it is more long-lasting; for example, **virtue** and **knowledge**. For branches of knowledge are more permanent and difficult to displace. Dispositions, however, are among those things that are easily changed. The difference between them concerns whether we possess something or do not yet possess it in relation to virtues. For a habit (such as the tendency toward temperance) is not easily changed. But those things that change quickly are called dispositions, such as anger, or grief, or sickness, or health. There are similar things. The **affections** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe), or passions/emotions</note> are numbered among these; they form dispositions and not the reverse. For such things as are well-ordered, whether they are wicked or not wicked, or better or worse, concern the affections. But dispositions are governed by habits. To agree entirely, it is thus defined by way of habit. Good health or quality is managed as it was among the ancients. Injustice and quality are movements derived from the ancients.

The **second kind of quality** is **natural power** or **incapacity** <note>original: "φυσικὴ δύναμις ἢ ἀδυναμία"</note>. This refers to being able to act or to be acted upon easily. Hence, power belongs to those who are naturally capable. Conversely, incapacity belongs to those not having the power. To be ill, for instance, is due to a natural incapacity or the inability to resist being affected. <insert>That which is hard has a natural power not to be easily cut. ### Concerning Opposites.

Opposites are spoken of in four ways. First, there are relative opposites, which are opposites by reference; for example, the double and the half; the slave and the master; and similar things. Second, there are those opposed as contraries; for example, good and evil. Third, there are those opposed as **privation** and **possession** <note>stērēsis and hexis</note>; for example, blindness and sight, or deafness and hearing. Fourth, there are those opposed as contraries <note>The scribe repeats "contraries" here, but the text refers to the next class: contradictories.</note>; for example, white and black. Finally, there are those opposed as **statements**; for example, affirmation and negation; such as "he sits" and "he does not sit." Let us first speak about relative opposites. Contraries are not necessarily those that fall under the same genus; they differ, and thus they must be set against one another; nevertheless, the genus of each of them <insert>is also opposed</insert>. However, one of these exists in the other, as in the case of whiteness and blackness, health and disease, virtue and vice, and so on.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of logic, specifically focusing on the structure of the syllogism and the rules governing the three figures of Aristotelian logic.</meta>

The pairing derived from the six combinations according to the <term>subject</term><note>original: ὑποκείμενον (hypokeimenon) - that which is spoken about</note> and the <term>predicate</term><note>original: κατηγορούμενον (kategoroumenon) - that which is asserted about the subject</note>. This in turn is established according to the hypothesis. This process creates three figures.

**The first figure** occurs when the subject in the first premise is the predicate in the second. For example: Every animal is a substance. Every human is an animal. Therefore, every human is a substance.

**The second figure** occurs when the same term is predicated of both. For example: Every human is an animal. No stone is an animal. Therefore, no stone is a human.

**The third figure** occurs when the same term is the subject of both. For example: Every human is an animal. Every human is capable of laughter. Therefore, that which is capable of laughter is an animal.

The modes of the introduction of the premises depend on both quantity <note>i.e., whether a statement is "all" or "some"</note> and quality <note>i.e., whether a statement is "is" or "is not"</note>. These are given as universal rules for each of the figures and modes.

**The first rule** is that from particular instances, or from indefinite statements, or from a negation, a <term>syllogism</term><note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> does not occur. One of the two must be <unclear>affirmative</unclear>.

**The second rule** is that from two negative statements, a syllogism cannot be produced. It is necessary <margin>concerning these</margin> to lead one of these to be affirmative.

**The third rule** is that if a premise is particular, the conclusion must also be particular. But the reverse is not necessarily true.

**The fourth rule** is that if one of them is negative, the conclusion must also be negative.

**The fifth rule** is that the major term never makes the conclusion a <unclear>syllable</unclear>.

---

### Concerning the First Figure

**The** first figure has the necessity of production, in which all these are correctly concluded through conversion. For the result produced from them is concluded because being predicated of the <unclear>whole</unclear> is the logic in the conclusion. Conversion necessarily falls so that the minor term is predicated of the major in the conclusion.

**Since** the premises come out together to form the whole of the first figure, six such rules are given:
<margin>letters</margin> **The first rule** is that in the first four modes of the first figure, the correct conclusions follow no particular <unclear>none</unclear> in genus.
<margin>unlettered</margin> **The second rule** is that in the same four modes, <margin>p p p barbara</margin> <note>A mnemonic for a syllogism with two universal affirmative premises</note> it does not follow from the other being negative.

**The first** mode of the first figure consists of two universal affirmative premises. It has a universal and affirmative conclusion in this mode.

# On the Third Figure:

<margin>
3rd Figure
destroys <note>Likely referring to the "destruction" or invalidation of a premise or conclusion</note>
</margin>
From this, it is established following a negative and a particular universal <note>The author is discussing the combination of premises in a syllogism</note>. They conclude a particular negative in this manner: No man is a stone. And man is an animal. Therefore, not every animal is a stone. And this is reduced to the 4th [mood] of the 3rd figure by the conversion of the affirmation within it. Regarding the particular negative syllogisms that reach a conclusion, the following rule is given: A syllogism concluding a particular negative, when converted, cannot conclude a universal. But when concluding it directly, it cannot conclude through itself when converted. In the 1st figure, every kind of proposition is concluded: such as universal, particular, affirmative, and negative. In the second figure, the universal and particular negative are concluded. In the 3rd figure, the particular affirmative and negative are concluded.

0 <note>Possibly a marker for a null result or a new section</note>
</margin>
Since we stand upon those analytical pairings concerning <term>terms</term> <note>original: "horoi" (ὅροι); the basic components of a logical proposition</note> which the conclusion follows from the premises being true, because of the couplings of the terms in which the truth of the pairs does not hold, it is therefore necessary to recognize such a coupling of terms. Thus, whenever there is a <term>useless pairing</term> <note>original: "achrestos syzygia" (ἄχρηστος συζυγία); a combination of premises that yields no valid logical conclusion</note> within the pre-defined rules of the syllogism, one must take one term as particular under the other. For example: "white." Under one: "horse." Again, this: "donkey," "animal." Through which [it is] a term. For example, when one is predicated of the other through something else. In <term>conversion</term> <note>original: "antistrophe" (ἀντιστροφή); the logical process of swapping the subject and predicate</note>, the whole truth of them must be converted. For example: "man," "capable of laughter," "donkey." Or: "man," "animal," "donkey." Through which [it is] a term. Again, when one is predicated of the other by a change of conversion. Or even a change of conversion with something foreign to both. For example: "man," "capable of laughter," "stone." Or: "man," "animal," "stone." Through these three stated rules, whatever weaving occurs and through whatever term—whether of quality or of some other categories—the terms are rendered incomparable, through which the useless pairing will appear not to hold. And one must always use these terms in the analyses concerning terms in which the conclusion does not follow. For it is not because the pairing is useless [in itself], but because the qualities of the terms are not in the same [category].

## Concerning the Argument <note>original: "epicheirema" — a dialectical or rhetorical argument</note>.

Reason <note>original: "logos" — can mean word, reason, account, or ratio</note> is spoken of in many ways. For first, the Reason of the universe is the same as the individual, even in appearances. As in the case of synonyms where the name is common, the "reason of the essence" <note>the definition</note> according to the name is the same. In the second way, Reason is the same as the definition <note>original: "horismos"</note>; hence definitions are also called "reasons." In another way, Reason is that which exists alongside the form of the matter. Just as in a knife, the iron is the matter, while the <margin>—</margin> required form is in the same thing, yet remains whole. <insert>e</insert> In this way, Reason is the essence of the definition of that which is predicated of many things. As we have seen in the pairings of reasons before us. Beyond this essential sense of Reason, it is noted that nothing leads away the conclusion. And according to the third way, Reason is taken instead for the definition of the **argument**. And this is the definition: an **argument** is a reason creating conviction <note>original: "pistis"</note> in a disputed matter. That is, a middle term leading to a conclusion. He, therefore, who employs the argument itself—for a conclusion in an argument or in arguments is demonstrative to those being persuaded. Which things, if not demonstrated, are disputed. It belongs to an inquiry of a doubted premise, not having the power to be understood on its own. But a true demonstration is an argument based on agreed-upon terms. This argument is a clear reason. The argument is plain to those who have learned and to the demonstrations. For while some things are taken in the showing but not understood, such an argument, because of the signs, cannot demonstrate the conclusion. Hence, whenever it is sought to be an argument, nothing is recognized.

An image <note>original: "εἰκὼν"</note> by the power of demonstration is the conclusion; and demonstration is such a discourse (and the case is more frequent and they are gathered together in a concluding manner, while those through figures are gathered by names; this is the most foreign form of belief <note>The author is likely discussing the "figures" of a syllogism, which are the different ways terms can be arranged.</note>). On the contrary, induction is a form of reasoning. In enthymemes, one uses demonstration, but in most cases, it is not a formal syllogism that creates the concurrence of ideas. Induction <term>Induction (epagoge): reasoning from specific instances to a general conclusion</term> is the departure from particulars toward universals; for example, that Socrates runs; every man runs, and thus the conclusion for all: "therefore every man runs." **An enthymeme is an incomplete syllogism;** <note>original: "ἐνθύμημα δέ ἐστι συλλογισμός ἀτελής"</note> that is, a discourse in which not all the parts are placed, but mostly the conclusion; for example, "every animal runs; therefore every man runs." For here, the missing part would be "every man is an animal." The syllogism is neither a premise nor a conclusion in itself, but the end result of the process. It should be known that the enthymeme requires a reading of the syllogism in this way: in every enthymeme there are two terms, just as in the syllogism. One of these is not placed in the conclusion, while the other remains; hence the relationship to those terms. The quantity in the conclusion does not create a multitude. Of these two terms, the one that is missing is supplied by the enthymeme. The remainder is stated once; nothing of what is said once, which contains the major term, is shown as one, but rather as equal to the sequence of the mode. And thus the enthymeme becomes a syllogism; for example, in this enthymeme: "every animal runs, therefore every man runs," the "man" and the "runs" are taken up; but "animal" is the half-term. This indefinite term "man" is missing once; as in this brief example, in which there is one premise: "every man is an animal"; and then the end will be a syllogism, thus: "every animal runs; every man is an animal; therefore every man runs." **By proverbs** <note>original: "παροιμίαις"</note> **one may demonstrate through enthymemes, or rather through the particular.** In these cases, it is principally agreed upon; so that they translate into myths <note>or fables</note> those things expressed enthymematically, as is the case with the Corinthians, and an enthymeme is necessary; it is a certain unfolding, which we held in a similar way. These same matters (in a Bacchic sense) are not so; hence even in the definition, this is its action. For demonstration exists through use. And the action itself is such as to be persuasion <term>Persuasion (peithein): the primary goal of rhetoric, distinct from scientific proof</term> through use; and there is yet more...

An inquiry, therefore, and a premise <insert>it follows then that a premise is an inquiry, while a conclusion is the result</insert> are the same in essence. **The Topic** <term>Topic: original "Topos," a "place" or starting point for an argument</term> **is divided** into the absolutely maximal premise and into the maximal premise derived from what is advantageous. **The maximal part of it** is that which is truly the greatest in itself. A maximal premise is one that is derived from self-evident things and from other things that are most well-known. Of these wholes, some are specific to nothing else. For that of which the species is predicated, the genus is also predicated of it. And that of which the definition is predicated, the thing defined is also predicated of it.

**The topic of the maximal difference exists in a single maximal difference among them.** For example, for the sake of argument: that of which the species is predicated, the genus is also predicated of it. And that of which the definition is predicated, the thing defined is also predicated of it; but the "topics" from which they are composed differ. For while these are the directed maximal points, one is composed from the species, and the other from the definition.

In general, these topics are called "simple": the differences of the maximal points. And thus the topic—the maximal point, the boundary, and the difference of the maximal point—are agreed to be a "topic." Therefore, for the use of those primarily concerned with **arguments** <term>Arguments: original "epicheiremata," a type of dialectical syllogism</term>, the topic is taken in a typical sense within an inquiry. This is derived from the types concerning "place" <note>original: "topos" can mean both a physical place and a logical topic</note> in the works on Physics. For the topic itself provides confirmation in physical evidence, and just as it exists from its being, so too the topic is agreed upon in the realm of thoughts for the sake of arguments.

**For that which is the difference of the maximal point is divided into the first topic derived from it**, the one from things prior, and the middle. **The first, then,** is that which is taken from things used as causes, from which it is possible to see whether the topic of the thing exists or not, such as from a definition. **The one from things posterior** is that which is taken from things used as causes from which it is possible to see from the power or from the motions, such as from the definition. **The middle, which is the primary one,** is that which is taken from things used as causes from which, and everywhere at hand, the essence of things is found. For example, from opposites. Immediately, the humble nature of spiritual things is sought; or from opposites in this way: as many as are poor—

This place is of the kind described. For sometimes the "all" is attempted from the part, which is the contemplation of the entire whole—for instance, starting from a part of a man. The proof from the whole is taken as if in contemplation, and through these, they call the whole something else; just as Plato <note>original: "Πλάτων"</note> himself calls it the "cause." <meta>This page continues a philosophical inquiry into the nature of the "Good" and the "End," likely following a discussion on the definitions of virtue and utility. The text focuses on the relationship between an object's purpose and the morality of its use.</meta>

The end <note>original: "telos" — the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing</note> toward which a thing tends is good; if the use of something leads to a good end, then that use is desirable, and the thing itself is good. Consequently, if the use of a thing is directed toward an end that is not good, but evil <note>original: "poneron" — wicked, worthless, or harmful</note>, then the thing itself is evil. Conversely, both the use derived from an end and that which results in an end can be evil. Furthermore, the disposition <note>original: "schesis" — the state or relation of a thing</note> of a thing also relates to its very being or will. That which pertains to life exists in a certain state, and its habit <note>original: "hexis" — a stable quality or character trait</note> or disposition is concerned with its own proper function <note>original: "ergon" — the specific work or task a thing is designed to do</note>. Moreover, use is not always a matter of necessity or compulsion. For example, the coming-into-being <note>original: "genesis"</note> of a house is something within our power; thus, it is good. Therefore, regarding coming-into-being: if the use of a thing is good, the thing itself is good. The coming-into-being of a thing by the will of a master is desirable; if the maker is good, his creation is good. But if that which is being produced is evil, its coming-into-being is also evil. <margin>18</margin> Destruction <note>original: "phthora" — decay or corruption</note> and the things resulting from what is produced are also considered; that which pertains to destruction is whatever relates to its own proper function, whether it be non-necessary or compelled. For instance, if attaining wisdom <note>original: "phronesis" — practical wisdom or prudence</note> is good, then the lack of it is evil. Thus, regarding destruction: if the use of being and of being wise is good, then destruction itself is evil. Where the use of wisdom would be evil, then destruction would be good. The opposite holds true regarding what is beneficial. The use of circumstances, therefore, occurs as in prosperity and good fortune, or in circumstances of goodwill and strife. To be fortunate is much more a matter of prevailing; it is not merely equality nor is it excess; it is likewise a matter of one's nature <note>original: "genos" — kind or lineage</note>. That which pertains to use itself is a disposition concerning that which comes into being through use—for example, equality in relation to proportion—because all things that come into being are good. Hence, where there is a need arising from use: if the use is good, the thing itself is good; but where the use is evil, the thing itself is evil. Common accidents <note>original: "symbebekota" — non-essential properties or chance events</note> are understood in two ways: some follow from one another, while others follow from these upon secondary things. Thus, it is clear that what happens (either from the same sources) to us are those things which commonly happen to the parts; so that these accidents are manifest. Therefore, from these, commonalities are to be taken in relation to one another. That which pertains to common accidents is a disposition distinguished from the accidents of the many; and some are not necessary...

The following text continues the discussion of logical "topics" (commonplaces or methods of argument), likely based on or commenting upon Aristotle’s *Topics*.

# On Logical Topics

The topic based on **similarity** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁμοίου"</note>. The greatest principle is that the same conviction applies to similar things. Those who wish to refute an argument do so in this way: if a statement is made about "the capable of laughing" regarding humans, one might say the same regarding "the capable of grammar." But if "the capable of laughing" does not apply to non-humans, then "the capable of grammar" does not apply to horses.

The eighth topic is also from **similarity**. The greatest principle is that if one of the similar things does not exist, then the other does not exist, nor do the rest.

From **analogy** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἀναλογίας"</note>, a conclusion is drawn when a comparison is required against something else. For example: as the pilot of a ship is to the ship, so the ruler of a city is to the city. For if the pilot of a ship is not chosen by lot <note>A reference to the Athenian practice of choosing officials by random lottery</note> but by skill, then the ruler of a city should also not be chosen by lot, but should learn through the work of skill. The eighth topic of analogy: the greatest principle is that the same judgment applies to proportional things.

The seventh topic is from **particulars** taken toward the **whole**, and likewise for things that exist by nature in relation to these. In these, the relationships are found. And if one is simple, the greatest principle is that where there is a name and a definition <note>original: "λόγος" (logos), here meaning the explanatory statement or definition of a word</note> in what they signify, there is a certain similarity following the sign of good things. For it is not always taken from itself, but from elsewhere. When the one who is ready to perform takes it, the definition would not be taken against the person to whom it is spoken instead of the second absurdity, when ignorance looks away. For example, that which relates to "the capable of laughing" and the action of those who breathe. The name and the definition are the same.

And this **substitution** <note>original: "μεταλλαγὴ" (metallage)</note> instead of the name is simple. The topic of substitution: the substitution of a name occurs when the name is greater or lesser [in scope], and one takes the phrase instead of the name. This would be from the name, as when "the philosopher does not envy." And one takes a substitution regarding "the virtuous man does not envy." And this substitution is taken regarding the name. For "the virtuous man does not envy" always holds, and he did not posit another relationship of greater or lesser. For example: "the wise man does not envy; therefore, the philosopher does not envy."

The eighth topic of **participation** <note>original: "μεταλήψεως" (metaleipsis), a technical term in logic for shifting the terms of an argument</note>. The greatest principle: whenever something fits a subject, and the name and the case-ending are lesser, the same fits this subject as both the name and the phrase.

<margin>2</margin> From this it is clear that the name is about the [definition]. For the definition takes each thing as a name he has written. Why then did he interpret the name? For example: "the philosopher is the one who practices philosophy."

Each of these causes exists for its own sake by nature. And this, in turn, is divided. For example, among living beings, one is without aim. Another is irrational.
