# Philosophy is a Gift

<margin>
What is philosophy? <note>original: "τί ἐστι φιλοσοφία"</note>
</margin>

Since **dialectic** <note>The art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logical argument.</note> is a method concerned with discourses, and of these, some are the resulting types and forms while others are the instruments by which it is distinguished in **logic** <note>original: "λογικῇ"</note>, we must record all these things so that the definition of this art does not fail by being too far removed from its goal. These instruments are for the rational considerations of things, and nothing foreign should be included. For both the labor of assigning causes and the efforts in logic or in the cessation of each task belong to the same field, rather than coming from different sources. We see those who teach each subject as a goal aiming at **reasoning correctly** <note>original: "ὀρθῶς συλλογίζεσθαι"</note> and likewise communicating with others in a different way. But one cannot be practiced in each alone if they use a position for the sake of this reasoning, while considering this to be the goal. For if one does not know their own position, they cannot direct a syllogism <note>A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> toward another, nor even toward themselves, unless they consider the whole matter or grasp it according to an opinion in their reflections. Since, therefore, it has been heard that one should communicate with others for this reason, syllogisms can be grasped; or rather, not the opinion of the predicates of **demonstration** <note>original: "ἀπόδειξις"</note>. These are called our syllogisms, but not within dialectic. We, however, take the name of discourse in these matters, for it is written concerning them. At that time, then, even a single person may be added. And for this reason, regarding the syllogisms occurring in discourses, we first examine the nature of discourse itself.

**Dialectic** is the syllogistic art of **self-evidence** <note>original: "ἐναργείας"; refers to clarity or intuitive certainty</note> directed toward another person, and nothing is based on suspension of judgment. Since, therefore, it uses self-evidence in discourse, one must not think of the syllogism of discourse as merely an instrument, but as the syllogism itself, by which the most brilliant points of opinion are grasped as definitions. Not only this, but also the opposite—learning clear things—is separated from those things according to dialectic. For this is the unique property of the syllogism: that which comes about clearly through reasoning. We call the meeting of one person with another "discourse." Because of this, it would not be assigned elsewhere in the writings on dialectic. There will be a certain difference in the reflection by which the same person reasons with themselves about those things which they are bound to define. For the result of discourse is understood as a "sweet definition" <note>original: "γλυκὺς ὅρος"; likely a metaphor for a satisfying or harmonious conclusion</note> or the goal of immediate things. And through this, it is distinguished from the syllogism of **practical** <note>original: "πρακτικῆς"</note> matters, which are not led toward signifying the...

<margin>Sophistry</margin> <note>original: σοφιστική</note> deals only with opinion concerning things that appear falsely. For every opinion is already something different [from truth]. It is either dialectical, or examination-based, or sophistical. On the one hand, the **didactic** <note>or "instructional" method</note> belongs to the realm of demonstrative proofs. It deals with accepted opinions <note>term: *endoxa* (ἔνδοξα) — reputable or widely held beliefs used as premises in reasoning</note> and things that seem true, proceeding from true and familiar principles, and it is through these that the analyses of the argument are produced. It also knows how to provide examples in this way, and its strength is not found in those who are merely learning.

**Dialectical** reasoning, on the other hand, is that which reasons simply from accepted opinions and appearances, but does not do so concerning the truth. "Accepted opinions" are therefore said to be those things which seem true to everyone, or to the majority, or to the wise; and among the wise, either to all of them, or the majority, or the most famous.

**Examination-based** <note>original: πειραστικὸν</note> reasoning is that which takes the opinions held by the person answering <margin>Sophistry</margin> through the things considered to be true within a specific art.

**Sophistical** reasoning is that which considers wisdom based on mere opinion. For the Sophist would take his starting points from these things, which constitute a "seeming wisdom" <note>original: νομιζομένη σοφία</note>. He holds nothing regarding the demonstrations of these matters or of things to come. Once he assumes the persona of a teacher of power, as is his custom, these premises themselves become his "demonstrations," provided we are able to speak the truth regarding his greatest propositions. From these, one sees that his power is directed toward the acquisition of money. For he does not possess the things he speaks of. For as much as a man is—insofar as it is possible to grasp the principles—all that is his power belongs to the appropriate knowledge and to that in which there is still either correctness of character, or of the end <note>the goal or *telos*</note>, and of reputation. Or rather, it is once and for all a matter of truth.

And the Sophist would not have grasped demonstrations, as if in the power of the proposed subject, which pertains to the genus and everything within opinion and reputation; and it is in opinion that he is beheld. For even their practical wisdom <note>term: *phronesis* (φρόνησις) — practical or ethical wisdom</note> does not neglect—let us leave aside for the present the task of discussing the Sophists more justly. Sophistry is blamed for looking toward a certain reputation for wisdom, but not for occupying itself with sophisms; rather, it hunts for a "seeming" wisdom. And because of this, it is not just a matter of love of strife or competition, for the deception would not come from those things alone. It is not merely that Sophistry is a certain deception of discourse, but that the Sophist is a deceiver by virtue of his pretense. # On the Topics of Sophistical Arguments

Regarding the topics of sophistical arguments and the methods by which the Sophists <note>Sophists were professional teachers in Ancient Greece often accused of using clever but fallacious reasoning to win arguments.</note> attack, they attempt to threaten those who provide answers. These methods are five in number: **Refutation**, **Falsehood**, **Paradox**, **Solecism**, and driving the person they are conversing with into a state of <term>babbling</term> <note>original: "endoloschia" (ἐνδολοσχία) - a technical term for forced repetition or redundant talk in logic.</note>.

**Refutation** is an obvious concession, or the denial of something previously conceded within the same dialogue, according to the force of the argument. For example, when the person answering denies what they agreed to just a short time before. The Sophist generally attacks in this way—as the saying goes regarding a deaf person: "They eat raw meat. Therefore, they eat raw meat." <note>This appears to be a fragmented or corrupted example of a circular argument or a failure in communication.</note> By this rule of argument, the respondent, having conceded what they later denied, is refuted. There are five modes of this argument: for the obscurity is resolved into the **Syllogism** <note>A formal logical argument consisting of two premises and a conclusion.</note>; or a **Seeming Refutation**; or one appearing in a syllogism and being practiced; or a **Syllogism of Contradiction**. This is of concern in the same discussion, and not just in the power of the argument, but it looks specifically at everything conceded. The concession is the [joining] of assertions, where one has been deceived by another. <insert>†</insert>

**Falsehood** occurs when, as these things are fulfilled, something false appears. In a concession, the one defending themselves is tripped up by the power of the Sophist's argument. For example, if they should say: "Everything hidden is refuted. The eye is hidden. Therefore, the eye is refuted."

<margin>**Paradox** is that which is contrary to the opinion of all people. Or it is to be [colored] because it is contrary to the opinion of the many.</margin>

However, it is not contrary to the opinion of *everyone*. For example, the idea that a star is larger in its power than the earth. And to be full, and to be [wild/beastly], and worthy, and a failure, or sinful. In terms of power, someone is sophistically wronged by nature. Just as it might happen that the King wins, while they have met with misfortune. "It happened that the King won while meeting with misfortune. Therefore, the King is unfortunately winning."

**Solecism** is a vice in the phrasing of syllogisms, resulting in something contrary to the art of Grammar. For example: <term>white man</term> <note>original: "anēr leukē" (ἀνήρ λευκή) - using a feminine adjective with a masculine noun.</note> and <term>man are running</term> <note>original: "anēr trekhousai" (ἀνήρ τρέχουσαι) - using a plural feminine verb with a singular masculine noun.</note>. Regarding the spoken word, they say the sophistical method works like this: "Those who teach under a curse speaking." Therefore, this is not speech. This does not comply with the rules of grammar.

It must be understood that the first type <gloss>of those found in speech</gloss> is analyzed as homonymy <note>original: "homonymia"; the use of the same word for different things</note>, a term beginning with things that are named. <note>original: Περὶ ἀμφιβολίας (Peri amphibolias). Ambiguity refers to a whole phrase having multiple meanings, whereas homonymy refers to a single word.</note>

Just as **homonyms** <term>homonyma: words that sound the same but have different meanings</term> have the power to resolve fallacies, so **ambiguity** is the form that yields the same expression but signifies several things. Ambiguity <note>original: amphibolia</note> is named from "walking around" <note>amphis</note> or "walking in two ways" <note>amphoteros bainein</note>. So that "walking around" is like becoming "around" something. And indeed, ambiguity in these cases yields either an expression <note>logos</note> or a name.

<margin>This differs from ambiguity in that, just as with one who has been baptized <note>likely a metaphor for being "immersed" or "overwhelmed" by a word's meanings</note>, everyone makes the same argument to one another, often doing so in different ways and signifying different things by the expression.</margin>

# On the Figures of Speech

For many things in the forms of syllogisms <note>logical arguments</note> are taken from the **figure of speech** itself, which is not reasonable; and from the similarity of one word to another, people concede that they are the same. But from the mere fact of "writing back" <note>original: *anagrapho*</note> and other such things which do not have a similarity in the word itself, some say there is a certain similar comparison in the word. And this seems to create a mode of meaning, even though those things do not possess the same substances. And that person seems to signify that they would not be the same, such as an "atom" <note>literally "indivisible"</note>. But the similarity in the word occurs after the removal of the names, so as not to suffer some error; yet it will be according to the extremities of the word, that is, the difference of those three <note>likely referring to the three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter</note>, as if it were a target. And the custom here is not such as one ought to believe, which also appears thus: that in this fourth section there is no proper reasoning, for many times when a verb is used, it is imagined otherwise. Therefore, even in the case of names that wander from the truth of the thing, it creates riddles of meaning within them, which would seem irrational.

**In the imagination** of this matter, since there is a similarity of the word in some cases to the opposite image; for the origin of the word does not signify from the thing in all cases. For example, if even the "not long ago" belongs to this matter; and before those other prior things, they signify a certain comparison as if taking them for nothing, toward signifying either feminine or neuter; such as "the all" <note>neuter: *to pan*</note>, as for example <unclear>properly</unclear> "all" the many things. But this one is said to be a "man" <note>masculine</note>, but not the things within. Therefore, even in these introductions, the choosing belongs to the choice.

**The accusative case** <note>original: *ho aitiatikos*</note> speaks toward being "this one" <note>masculine</note>; because the words signifying an opinion in the speech in each **category** <note>term: *kategoria* — Aristotle's classification of types of being, such as substance, quality, or action</note>, will all seem to me to be certain things in relation to other categories. <meta>This page continues the analysis of logical fallacies, specifically focusing on the transition from linguistic fallacies (fallacies of expression) to those independent of language (material fallacies).</meta>

Regarding the unchangeable nature of place, the argument sometimes arises from the **figure of speech** <note>original: "σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως" — a fallacy where the grammatical form of a word misleads one about its actual category of being</note> so that a shift in categories occurs. This happens in relation to what is signified by the actual thing, but the deception arises through the manner of the specific wording. For instance, "movement" signifies "at some time," as do "always" and "they are toiling." Therefore, it does not signify itself as a "when" <note>the category of Time</note> in the same way that "to be healthy" does; rather, it signifies "to act" <note>the category of Action</note>. Yet "to act" also signifies itself. Thus, it signifies itself in the same way as "to act." The fallacy involving "always" is a **figure of speech**; for you see "as always" in the same time, and when you see "whiteness," you then see "whiteness." But this is not a formal syllogism. The external **figure of speech** works like this: "white" is the "when" from which you see "whiteness."

**The third mode occurs when it happens that something signifying a quality is treated as a "this-something"** <note>original: "τόδε τι" — a specific, individual substance or entity</note>. It happens that the "this-something" and the "this-something" occurring are, as it were, reversed, yet it is itself a "this-something." It can signify a "quality" <note>original: "ποιόν"</note>, while the thing signified and the one knowing it involve "more" or "equal" things; of necessity, it must be in the same manner. Indeed, the "this-something" does not signify a "quality" in relation to quality; for if the "of what sort" <note>the qualitative nature</note> is left behind and what is in it remains, and if one is accustomed to quality, one might reason that it is not a "this-something." The individual case is not in it in that manner. The fallacy is shaped thus: "Socrates is a man; 'man' is a genus; therefore, Socrates is a genus" in relation to himself. But this is not the case; for the genus does not derive from the same basis as Socrates. Thus, the "of what sort" shifts into the "this-something." The "of what sort" cannot produce deception except because it is a habit for some of those who know. For example, saying: "Man is a genus; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is a genus." Every such case would be due to the linguistic hypothesis acting as an oversight, shifting from the "of what sort" <note>the universal quality</note> to the "this-something" <note>the individual</note>.

In sophisms outside of language, then, the cause of the error arises through the unity of the sound—if, for instance, two or more things are signified through the sound. # Boethius

<margin>
**That regarding the** thing signified by these words, this matter makes the arguments; and every announcement is called a declaration. The same follows: the "rational animal"—for example, that "man" is composed of other things, just as the origin of "self-moving" is a property within the "rational."
**But that the** conclusion is the "animal" in a statement; for it contains the proof from another. Then the statement is also a cessation. Either it is the same as itself, or the question of the statement arises; then the statement is also called a **problem** <note>original: *problēma*</note>. For example: "if man is an animal." As for the statement: having produced conviction, thus the statement is a problem; it is necessary.
</margin>

A **premise** <note>original: *protasis*</note> is a statement signifying what is true or false. For example, in some way or another, "man is an animal." This is also a statement <note>original: *apophansis*</note>. And every announcement is called a **problem** when the premise is brought forward for the sake of doubt and ambiguity. For example: "Is life a property of man?" A **conclusion** <note>original: *symperasma*</note> is a premise proven through a syllogism. For example: "Is life necessary for man?" demonstrating the facts. **Then, a statement** is called an announcement only when it stands alone; but when something else is brought forward, it is a proof; and the problem exists upon the statement itself; and these in turn have a conclusion. Therefore, a statement, a premise, a problem, and a conclusion are the same thing; but they differ in the manner of their expression. An **enthymeme** <note>or "argument"; original: *epicheirēma*</note> is a discourse producing conviction regarding a doubtful matter. A **topic** <note>original: *topos*; literally "place"</note> is the discovery of an argument; and when this is in agreement with the proposed problem, it is called a fitting argument.

One must recognize that premise and problem, conclusion and statement, will be found to be the same thing under a single reality, differing only in relationship. For when we wish to construct a syllogism, and we include them in relation to something, the syllogism is called a premise. For example: "If any soul is self-moving; that which is self-moving is always in motion; therefore the soul is always in motion." Behold, "the soul is self-moving" and "always in motion" are the syllogism's premise. But when we take it up because of a difficulty, such as "Is the soul self-moving?", the whole thing becomes a problem. When one proves that the soul is self-moving, or even when it is known that everything is self-moving, it is the same. But when one concludes thus: "The soul is [not] unmoved; the unmoved is self-moving; therefore the soul is self-moving," it is a conclusion. A statement <note>original: *apophansis*</note> occurs when I simply declare something about something, or something away from something. Such as "Man is an animal" or "Man is not a horse."

Regarding arguments and topics, Boethius has spoken above. But we, taking our starting points here, speak briefly as follows. It is asked whether arguments are more valuable than topics. It is resolved thus: if the problem is stated and resolved, the topics are more valuable. And again, regarding the one in doubt: from where will one reason out these things? By finding how the selected elements happen to be; and next, whether the arguments belong to these. For those things that happen to be syllogistic are stable. Again, stable things are more valuable than those being made; just as the springs of unremembered arguments are more valuable than the arguments themselves. We must find what kind of ambiguity we have; this and such things are the arguments.

Thus, he says, let each of the mentioned things be examined in the books. It is the nature of these things to be interwoven according to species, parts, and figures. And first, we must distinguish the nature of the proposition. The proposition itself, therefore, is a statement <gloss>signifying</gloss> (marking) truth or falsehood. Of this, there are two species: one is affirmation, and the other is negation. Affirmation is when one speaks thus: **Man is an animal.** Negation is that which utters thus: **Man is not an animal.**

---

Of these, some were universal, others particular, others indefinite, and others singular <note>original: *kathekasta*, referring to individuals</note>. Universal propositions are those that propose twice in this way: **Every man is just. No man is just.** Particulars are those which are proposed in this manner: **Some man is just. Some man is not just.** Indefinites are thus: **Man is just. Man is not just.** Singulars are those that reach down to individual persons, such as: **Cato is just. Cato is not just.** For Cato is one of the individuals and a singular instance.

---

Of these, some are called categorical and others hypothetical. Categorical are those which are proposed simply, or those in which no power of hypothesis occurs in that manner. As when one simply says the genus: "He is rational." If a hypothesis is woven from this, it becomes one hypothetical proposition out of two propositions, in this manner: **If man is rational, he is an animal.** For if there are hypotheses in the extension, it is so that man is absolutely understood to be an animal, or not.

# On Logic and Truth

Truth is woven together, firm and unchangeable. Whether it is sought after or remains at rest, its form is one; for the truth of truth is always one, not existing as something belonging to things, but existing eternally. Just as he who is old creates old things, and he who builds is a builder, so too do all these arguments work together <note>original: "συνωφελούν"</note> as they are gathered through them. Therefore, if God [were the cause of] evil, he would be evil, as previously demonstrated. For the cessation of evil does not naturally belong to Him, as I perceive it; for virtue and love itself are contrary to these things. Our escape from passion is gathered in a unified way.

Therefore, having spoken concisely about these two as if they were principles and having made use of them, they are encompassed in a certain manner. One is the subject of the **syllogism** <term>syllogism: a formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>, and the other of **induction** <term>induction: reasoning from specific instances to a general law</term>. In these, all people find them ready at hand as if they were inhabitants [of the mind]. For the rule comes from the syllogism, while the other comes from induction from the beginning. For either this will fulfill the syllogism or the conception of those who know.

<margin>Note: An argument <note>epicheireme</note> and an **enthymeme** <term>enthymeme: a "truncated" syllogism where one premise is unstated or implied</term>. For the cause was that which is held by art concerning the underlying matter. For both the power and the act do not look at our resulting enthymeme in this way.</margin>

And the **enthymeme** is an incomplete syllogism; at least in cases where not all the premises are drawn from the truth so that the conclusion follows through them. For example, if someone were to say: "Man is an animal; therefore he exists." For it misses the other premise entirely, which would force a perfect conclusion. Since the enthymeme moves from the more universal toward the particular, it also observes its goal just as it is similar to the syllogism.

<margin>Enthymemes are formed from significant premises, or from irrational signs, or from things coming shortly into the stated difference. However, they are not a [full] syllogism. For clarity shows the underlying argument.</margin>

But insofar as the requirements of the syllogism do not always coincide for everyone, it differs from the reasoning in a syllogism. For this reason, it is called an **incomplete syllogism**. The **example** <note>paradeigma</note> likewise is most closely entwined with **induction** and differs from it in its conception. For the particular consequence of one part, when other particulars are not brought in, is woven together; it is gathered and conceded from the main point. For if the enthymeme moves with the part—for the difference is also there—likewise the equity of the principles remains indefinite in the description. But they shared the indefinite because it is not of a limit, and in color it is defined, whereas in induction some things are altogether defined; in which there is a rebuke.

The problem is one of **definition**. The maximal proposition is: if that which appears more likely to be the case is not, then neither would that which appears less likely be the case. ### Concerning the Category of the Accident

Both "co-ordinates" <note>original: "συστοιχίας" - words from the same root, like 'justice' and 'just'</note> and "inflections" <note>grammatical cases or endings</note> are shared by names signifying the same things. Just as with the term "justice," or "the just," or even "justly." From these things thus grasped, the matter is taken. For example, if from the saying that "to be happy" exists, we should say that beauty is joy, then one will also say that the good is joy.

### Concerning the Category of the Accident (continued)

A maximal proposition: those things in which the genera and causes are natures. For example, everything may arise from the genus. A "genus" <term>genus (genos): a class or category that includes several species</term> is that which is predicated of many and differing things in answer to the question "what is it?" From these, the species of the matter are encountered in this way. For example, if from the premise that fire is not a number, and that it moves itself—as the opinion of **Xenocrates** <note>Xenocrates (c. 396–314 BCE) was a head of the Platonic Academy who famously defined the soul as a "self-moving number."</note> states—we should say what the soul is like. For the soul is a self-moving number; that [soul] is a number.

### Concerning the Category of the Property
<note>The "Property" (idion) is a quality that belongs only to one species, but does not define its essence.</note>

For it belongs to the genus. A maximal proposition: those things whose genera are different, they themselves are likewise different. For the "property" is also predicated of more than one thing differing in number in answer to the question "what is it?" From this, the same matter arises for this genus. For example, if "color" is sought, we might say it is "white" in a subject. Both white and black are in a subject; but let nothing be classified as a property of it. The resulting problem is absurd: that every subject, in order not to be what it is, signifies some accident as an essence.

A maximal proposition in which the aforementioned species are observed within the genera—

# Page 74

Having thus described these matters, we must now speak concerning the <term>enthymeme</term> <note>a type of rhetorical syllogism or logical argument based on probabilities rather than certainties</note> derived from **division**. In these enthymemes, a comprehensive result does not occur due to the specific arrangement of the argument.

The <term>topos</term> <note>literally "place"; a "commonplace" or formulaic method for finding arguments</note> which is derived from definitions and subsequently from the whole, Themistius <note>a 4th-century Byzantine statesman and philosopher</note> proposed to be derived from **essence**. For it is established from that which has been defined. This [topos] exists either in the investigation of essence or is descriptive. In the passages of Cicero’s *Topics* <note>original: "Κικέρωνος Τοπικοῦ"</note> regarding evidential delivery, this topos is the same as the enthymemes of division found in the middle [categories] and those pertaining to division. For whenever we have a purpose of refutation and of facts, or whenever we derive proof from the delivery of the parts, we recognize division as <margin>3</margin> necessary for the <term>stasis</term> <note>the "point of issue" or the central question in a legal case</note>.

Division, which is derived from the whole, contains either evidence or proof. Therefore, the topos derived from the enthymeme of division was classified among the intermediate types by Dionysius <note>likely Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a teacher of rhetoric</note> in his *Rhetoric*, as it is said to originate from him. The statement of the topos is thus generalized as follows: *one must seek things according to their conjugation* <note>logical connections or related groupings</note>. Such a matter is that which is taken from the whole. The topos of the whole requires that the parts be sought according to themselves in this manner.

**Deceit** <note>original: "δόλος"</note> is shared [in this category]. When one does one thing and feigns another, having a defined manner of deceiving the mind. And from this, some of these things are truly characterized by deceit, or are hidden. God appears from within to be firm, not even using a shameful word as if it were decent.

From the **etymology** of a common saying, the topos is the same as previously stated. Having noted it from the name. That which Cicero derives from the **part**, the enthymeme from the **whole** is simultaneously the same. What Cicero calls "from the path," Themistius calls "from the part of <unclear>essence</unclear>."

# The Interpretation of Hermogenes

The interpretation of Hermogenes: from connected and common elements.
From the "genus" <note>The general category or class</note> of Cicero; from the whole of Hermogenes. From parts, as is common; from the "difference" <note>Specific distinguishing features</note> of Cicero. From the whole or from the part of Hermogenes. From the "opposite" of Cicero; the same corresponds to the "opposites" of Hermogenes. Those derived from "circumstances" <note>Accidents or non-essential qualities</note> in Cicero, and from "prior circumstances," belong to Hermogenes. From "consequences" and "results," partially more extensive. Those from "conflicting matters" in Cicero; the same functions from the "opposites" in Hermogenes. From the "judgment" of Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>; those from the "end" <note>The purpose or goal</note> of Hermogenes. When from the "comparison" of Tullius, some are in each category, while those of the "greater or lesser" belong to Hermogenes. The "comparison of equals" of Cicero; from the "similar" of Hermogenes.

Therefore, every most complete division <term>diairesis: a systematic logical or rhetorical classification</term> of Cicero and a certain single division of Hermogenes can be adapted and made to fit, yet not every part of Hermogenes' division, nor again can every part be brought into harmony with that of Tullius. One must not think that because something is left out in the division of Hermogenes, or when the writings appear to have a gap somewhere, that the division of Tullius—which is most complete for us—is being <unclear>taught</unclear> to <unclear>fit</unclear> them together; the divisions are necessarily <unclear>composed</unclear> from one another.

It is most fitting for us to both educate and rejoice no less, if indeed [the soul], having been separated from the many, is nourished by the divine words <note>original: "ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν θείων λόγων πινόμενην" - literally "drunk in" or "nourished by divine discourses"</note>. One must not consider these things merely useful for a man, but something radiant; and I desire [to strengthen] faith. Indeed, these things are necessary for all, but especially for the noble and good <term>kaloi kagathoi: the Greek ideal of gentlemanly virtue and beauty</term>, because they reflect the image of beauty and form, shining forth without folly. It is not the mark of wisdom to be humbled, and not only for the uneducated; these things are safeguards against deception. This [discourse] of goodwill and of that which is moved in God is far superior to all others, even in one's own failings. For if one is ready to acknowledge failings, you must consider that some diligence is required. Nevertheless, nothing from them is as it reasonably should be. But we also hold the doctrines of piety <note>original: "εὐσεβείας δόγματα"</note>, as many as do not fall short of any duties; so that even the essence of our humble nature, if it maintains its uprightness, is persuaded. First, for the most part, they do not seek the good from external things, but they employ every care, and we embrace all things so as not to suffer among the ineffective. So, it is reasonable to wish to know that these things apply to all. Why then [address] those who have endured the most excellent accusations? If there are disputed matters, let him attempt to resolve them.

By the memories of these things, O dear and most revered head <note>A classical Greek idiom for a beloved person, similar to "dear soul"</note>. And it is not at all the fault of the disciples. Or if it appears as some [ill] fortune to you, my dear daughter, who are both wise and beautiful, it seems like a barbarian form. For why should one not hope for the whole? Furthermore, not only does disease strike from [without]. But all the wisdom within me, desired by her from afar, belongs to those who are always preserved, and to the other acknowledged **Platonic philosophers** <note>original: "Πλατωνικῶν φιλοσόφων"</note>; it is difficult for those who are thus at a loss. 

Nevertheless, I will speak to you alone and to our whole company, knowing that grace is stirred up by your assistance, because you in no way demand the most pure interpretations <term>exegeseis: detailed critical explanations of a text</term>. For many have treated this very book in many writings, and especially **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a major Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>. # On the Categories

For all things that are well-known, it is necessary to establish their proper names, and these exist! <note>The author uses an emphatic tone regarding the existence of proper terminology.</note> Specifically, those names which belong to the scientific study of letters <note>original: "γραμμάτων" (grammaton); here referring to the basic elements of language or logic</note> are shown to be primary and significant. In this way, for instance, **Aristotle** sometimes follows the style of **Xenophon** in the character of his names—as he also does in his letters—varying the names themselves. At other times, however, he adopts those terms that are significant of the content for the purpose of instruction, aiming toward the understanding <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia)</note> and the induction <term>Induction (epagoge): the process of moving from specific examples to a universal conclusion</term> of the examples provided. Therefore, just as with that author, so too with this one, the names of the "Categories" were established among the ancients.

Regarding the **Categories**, many people desire to demonstrate and complete them based on what has been laid down, yet they are not yet truly philosophers of these things, nor do they simply signify the precision of the unchanging aspects of speech. The writing on the "Category" is clear, then: that specific voice <note>original: "φωνή" (phone); often used in logic to mean a spoken word or significant sound</note> signifies that the primary things among significant terms are predicated <note>original: "κατηγορεῖται" (kategoreitai); to be stated or asserted of a subject</note> of those things falling under them. And the significant words, the common ones, are predicated according to this entire description, not by the word alone. 

But since the Categories are named after the things predicated—because it is necessary for them to be said of some underlying subject <term>Subject (hypokeimenon): that which lies at the base of a proposition; the thing being talked about</term>—let us briefly demonstrate how this is so. For before considering any of the other matters, we must take care of the summary, so that we do not fall into difficulty because of a lack of clarity regarding the subjects before us. Since it seems to me to be a matter of doubt from where such a thing agrees—whether it is a **thing** <note>original: "πρᾶγμα" (pragma); a physical reality</note> or a **thought** <note>original: "νόημα" (noema); a mental concept</note>—let us examine these things clearly once again. 

One might answer briefly and directly that, primarily, the names are significant; but by accident <term>Accident (symbebekos): a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</term>, the things themselves are signified. Since there is much inquiry concerning the things spoken of—and I desire to speak even more concerning these same things—it appears that the passive states <note>original: "παθητικά" (pathetika)</note> are demonstrated in relation to one another, not without use for those things being discussed. Indeed, they do not enumerate these before the one and the same word, but they let these arguments go as they alter them. Even more so if one wishes to look at the things in which they consist. Such matters are apparent in the common opinion of life. 

It is necessary, therefore, to try to recognize everything said concerning the things predicated, which he has used with a certain fear through them. For some things harm and do not resolve the matters, while others are the things themselves; we do not only say what is correct. When we do not make a declaration, we might hold these things as cut off. But as for not being at a loss, I would wish for everyone to find this most easy.

# On the Nature of Expressions

These are, for the most part, instead of the significant words used in the arts <note>technical terminology</note>. Both of these together—those derived from speech—define the character of interpretation <note>original: "hermeneia," referring to the way thought is expressed in language</note>. For neither compound words, such as "the neighbor's boy," nor those added afterward <note>adverbs</note>, such as "dexterously," are included. Nor are those elegant words spoken through apocope <note>the cutting off of a final letter or syllable</note>, nor invented names, nor those used figuratively <note>original: "eschematismena," referring to rhetorical figures</note>, nor pronouns. Furthermore, whatever is considered specifically within the realms of poetry and rhetoric will nowhere fall under the Categories. For such things require a knowledge of phrasing and syntax separate from the present study.

The intention of the Categories is to convey the primary meaning of words, and the primary substances as they exist among real beings. These are observed in eternal terms <note>original: "rhemata"</note>. But they do not include those things observed as accidents to a substance which confuse our concepts. These <margin>these</margin> being figuratively formed, make "being" something terrible and incomprehensible, and are useless for knowing nature. Words that signify causes and the definitions of primary things easily drag down that which is fragmented into the infinite; they make the art <note>the system of logic</note> trivial or make it rare to accurately straighten out the nature of beings.

Therefore, these provide the most useful resources for recognition, especially cooperating with those who love learning and have mastered the art of discourse. Thus, a tropical <note>figurative</note> or metaphorical name—such as "to throw back the mane" <note>original: "anachaitison," a metaphor for rearing up or throwing off a rider</note>—and perhaps "to arrange," [are excluded]. But neither are the "modes" <note>particles/conjunctions</note>, such as "as" or "for the sake of" and such things, able to be included. Nor are the quantifiers <term>prosdiorismoi: logical determiners like "all" or "none"</term>, such as "every" and "no one." And the cause which is not a specific "something" will not fall under the Categories. For in none of such things is there contained a defined, individual nature.

For this reason, having been rejected by both [reason] and speech, he <note>likely Aristotle or the commentator</note> brings only this consideration of phrasing to the goal of the Categories. Whenever, therefore, it is not even toward truth through such a discourse, the "properly" and the "true" are situated in the nature of beings, among those things primarily belonging to the Categories. Therefore, whatever is written and named by the voice as a simple category concerning things that do not even exist—through a definition into a significant discourse concerning them—these things indeed <unclear>were shown</unclear>...

Since everything is a "this something," "nothing" is divided and spoken of in turn: one way as substance; another way as quality; and so on for the others.

But to which category does "He" belong? In itself, to none. Look. And what will one place as "worthy with me"? And "what it is" and the <term>Essence</term> <note>original: "to ti en einai"; literally "the what it was to be," a technical Aristotelian term for the definition of a thing's nature</note>, to what category do they belong? Each of these is also spoken of in two ways: for these are either substances in relation to substance; or quality in relation to quality; or quantity in relation to quantity; or substance in relation to something else, and so on for the rest. But meanings do not arise for you in every instance. For from quality, other things follow: "quality at some time"; "quantity"; and "quality in relation to something"; and from quality in this manner. (And from relation or in some way); (likewise for the rest in each case.)

Similarly also regarding the prepositions: either substance to substance; or quality to quality; or quantity to quantity; and so on for the rest. But conversely, there is again a greater analogy within it; what is each of the categories? Yes. How then is each demonstrated? One as substance; another as a certain quality; another as quantity; or another among the rest.

Does the <term>Definition</term> <note>original: "horos"; the boundary or formal statement of a thing's nature</note> reveal what a thing is? Most certainly. But what kind of thing does the definition reveal? The substantial <term>Characteristic</term> <note>original: "idiotes"; a specific property or quality</note>—the "of what kind" characteristic; and this is twofold. One as a genus-characteristic; another as "where"; another as "relation"; or another as "acting."

# On Simple and Combined Terms

Furthermore, just as an indivisible unit <note>original: "monad"</note> and a discrete quantity are measured by equals, so too must we state how things in the same genus are called "synonymous." Regarding **uncompounded** <note>original: "asyntheta"</note> things, then: they distinguish between those utterances made with combination and those without combination. For it is not the case that all things spoken are necessarily either with or without combination. For instance, the word "man" or "horse" is without combination, for it does not include a connective conjunction.

However, the phrase "man horse" <note>The author is likely distinguishing between a single noun and a list or a proposition lacking a verb</note> is not without combination. For verbs bind together certain syllables and elements of one another. Some people, therefore, who define "combination" <term>symploke: the weaving together of words to form a proposition</term> as an utterance involving a connective conjunction, follow the basic elements, using a method of analysis. 

And this was expressed in older writings <unclear>he said</unclear>, where they also named the gathering of several collections a "combination." On the other hand, regarding that which is without combination—such as "man" or "horse"—because it binds together and possesses each word made of certain syllables, it is not necessary to be constrained by it. For the <unclear>arguments</unclear> of the ancients regarding things in a collection did not concern syllables when they used the name "combination."

### On Place and Time

But one thing is in a **place** as a body is in a vessel, in relation to that which contains it; it would be something incorporeal were it to exist apart from the good. It is impossible for a body to be separated from where it is, just as a body is in a place or a "where"; it is simultaneously also in **time**. For it can neither be greater than it is, nor can it exist without time. And therefore, parts are not in time—or rather, they are only as far as they can be separated from time—but they are never truly separated from place and time; rather, they relate to whatever happens to be the case. 

The rule of common things is not established here in this way; nothing stands in opposition. That which is in a place is in both place and time. For that which is in time, according to its own nature, is that which is **moving** and **changing**. For it passes along with time and changes along with it. From this, we also derive the "eternal," and that which happens to be in time. Even if a thing were unmoved and immutable, if time exists, it remains within it. 

In this way, one might consider whether the moving or the unmoved would be fittingly associated with time, and from what source they are in time. Both are associated with the moving. Such, then, is the nature of the whole in relation to time. For it is not bodies that endure. So it is judged that one thing is in another. Thus it was said of old that a "part" comes to be in this way. Regarding the "uncompounded" in time, it must be spoken of more generally. But it shall be discussed where it is found.

# On Substance and its Parts

...substance into parts. <note>original: "τὴν οὐσίαν εἰς μέρος"</note> **Aristotle** resolved the second point, or rather the essential particular, by taking a difference within it. He says that everything with which the essential <term>essence (ousia)</term> is present is the same, so that according to him, they say these things exist: some things complete the substance by being within it, while others are not of such a kind and do not complete it. He says that participation itself is also of this nature. Just as one might say that color belongs to a subject <note>original: "ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ" - a technical term for a substrate or underlying thing</note> as a quality, it happens that those things in the subjects are distinct from the part. On the other hand, nothing of the other sort completes the substance.

But even so, the parts of the subjects are a greater portion. Even if it must come to the same thing, he can treat them as definitions of what is "in a subject." It is found also in particulars as if in a part, and indeed as a whole in parts. For the things in them follow our definition of being in a subject; for the whole is not immediately a part. Rather, some things are divided by part and others as a whole, so that substance is distinct from <term>accidents (symbebekota)</term> <note>accidents are non-essential properties, like being tan or sitting down, which can change without the thing ceasing to be what it is</note>.

In this way, it can also be in a whole; for since it is in the whole, it is also in the parts. For example, even if the whole is in all the parts, it is not a part of them. For they possess the whole alongside the things in the parts; thus they are inseparable from them. For it is common to all wholes. It is not only in a subject, but also the things within those things that are in a subject.

And yet again, according to our view, the <term>form (eidos)</term> <note>the "shape" or "intelligible structure" of a thing</note> is properly a part and exists at the end of the whole body; it is not, however, viewed in that way. Hence the Aristotelian principle: that which exists in the part must also exist in the whole. In this way, it also exists in the forms, though these classes of belief are being set aside. For the whole is in some one of the parts. But it is also viewed as the "all" in the parts.

From this, it was seen that the "in part" is like being in the subjects. Therefore, the whole which precedes the attached parts is the "portion" as a part. For not only is that which comes from the one a single part, but one might also assume the subject itself to be a part. For the whole is not taken to be in all the parts and their subject. And again, because the one has such a nature in its own forms, it is not even in any subject of them, so as to be an inseparable completion of the forms. There are many things concerning the qualities of the majority, and concerning such works. So that the opinion does not pass into the other part of those things which are "in subjects."

But do we say that the whole is in no way separated from the world? The things in substances exist as if they were separable. For the eternal things are separated from their own members of the form. Separable...

Furthermore, we introduce the common properties of beings in a manner similar to those things that fall under the natures and phenomena of these entities. This complex and conversational approach clearly defines a distinct field of study. First, we consider the primary **categories** <note>The fundamental classes of being, such as substance, quality, and quantity</note>, and those that demonstrate their developments so that they form a coherent account in themselves. These things depart through the whole; for again, they were universal before they were substances, being themselves accidents and intensifications, and admittedly supporting them. Their defining form is given universally to those things derived from a single source. And indeed, we are concerned with the sequence of the whole, which is clear; thus, he remarked that what is given is harmonized, and it is introduced again. But even from the neck and from there, we already reach for the immovable aspects of the forms, as if by a surgical hand.

There, however, the wall is entirely upon one thing. Just as in common beings, it has taken the first and most authoritative **substance** <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia); the core essence or "beingness" of a thing</note>. But before this, the **accidents** <note>original: "συμβεβηκότα"; properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size</note> exist. Having been so persuaded, thus: **1.**, because that was first questioned, let it be with difficulty. For while substance still existed, those things from Elea <note>Likely a reference to the Eleatic school of philosophy, such as Parmenides or Zeno</note> were not there; how might we know if it should join with them? For either this exists as common in both from that source; but it is unclear, like something else from this. For that which was not the body is not only ranked; so that either there is every battle of none, or the consequences are not only so.

Just as <gloss>or</gloss> the primary substances <note>original: "πρῶται οὐσίαι" (protai ousiai); the fundamental individual things like a specific person or horse</note> are called substances most of all because they underlie everything else and all other things are either predicated of them or exist in them; so also do the species stand in relation to the genera. <gloss>Or for there are difficulties regarding the species</gloss> but the species <insert>is prior to the genera</insert> and is more truly substance; for the species underlies the genus. For while the genera are predicated of the species, the species do not reverse and predicate of the genera. Therefore, from these facts, the species is more a substance than the genus. 

Of the species themselves, however, as many as are not genera, one is not more a substance than another; for a "certain man" <note>an individual human</note> is no more a substance than a "certain ox." Likewise, among primary substances, one is no more a substance than another; for the individual man is no more a substance than the individual ox. 

It is reasonable that, after the primary substances, only the species and the genera are called **secondary substances**; for only these define the primary substance among the things predicated. For if one were to explain what a "certain man" is, he would explain it properly by giving the species or the genus, and he will make the person more known by giving "man" rather than "animal." But of all other things one might give, he will be giving something foreign to the nature, such as giving "white" or "runs" or anything of that sort. Thus it is reasonable that these alone among the rest are called secondary substances.

Furthermore, the primary substances are called substances most of all because they underlie all other things and all other things are predicated of them or are in them. And as the primary substances relate to all other things, so the species relates to the genus; for the species underlies the genus. For the genera are predicated of the species, but the species do not reverse to the genera. Thus, from these points, the species is more a substance than the genus.

It is common to every substance not to be in a subject <note>original: "ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ" (en hypokeimeno); meaning it doesn't exist as a property of something else, like 'redness' exists in a 'ball'</note>. For the primary substance is neither in a subject nor is it said of a subject. Regarding the secondary substances, it is clear that they are not in a subject in the following way: "man" is said of a subject (the individual man), but is not *in* a subject; for "man" is not inside the individual man. Likewise, "animal" is said of a subject (the individual man), but is not in the individual man. 

Furthermore, of those things that are in a subject, nothing prevents the name from sometimes being predicated of the subject, but it is impossible for the definition to be so. However, for secondary substances, both the definition and the name are predicated of the subject; for you will call the individual man both "man" and "animal." Thus, substance would not be among the things in a subject. 

This, however, is not unique to substance, but the **difference** <note>original: "διαφορά" (diaphora); the specific characteristic that distinguishes a species, like "rational" for humans</note> is also among the things not in a subject. For "pedestrian" and "two-footed" are said of a subject (man), but are not in a subject; for "two-footed" is not *in* the man, nor is "pedestrian." Also, the definition of the difference is predicated of the subject; for example, if "pedestrian" is said of the man, the definition of "pedestrian" will also be predicated of the man; for the man is a pedestrian. 

Let us not be disturbed by the parts of substances, as if they were in the wholes as in subjects, lest we be forced to say they are not substances. For things "in a subject" were not defined as things belonging to something as a part. It also belongs to substances and differences that all things are said synonymously from them; for all the categories derived from them are predicated either of the individuals or of the species. In the case of **substance**, this is how it stands: for example, in the body and the individual substance, that which does not happen to have a form <note>Greek: *eidos*</note> is not the opposite of itself or the things within it; for it cannot be an opposite. But neither do they say that opposites belong to the "living being" <note>Greek: *zōon*</note>, nor does it possess anything as an opposite in this way. Among the species <note>Greek: *eidesin*</note>, there is nothing opposite to **substance**; for none of these is worthy of being an opposite. In most cases, and in those things that exist oppositely, such as the "greater" and the "small," all things are defined accordingly. Thus, this truly belongs especially to some particular thing and to its substance.

But concerning the whole of substances and the extremes: it is a **characteristic** <term>idion - a property unique to a specific category</term> of substance not to have opposites. For we shall not say that the same differences—those which are within the substance itself—constitute a definition. Thus, while it may happen that the "moist" and the "dry" exist as opposites to one another, this is not the case regarding whole substances, which he says possesses a characteristic opposition even in the case of **matter** <note>Greek: *hylē*</note> where they say it exists. 

However, this is not a unique characteristic of substance; for in many other things, it is the case that nothing is contrary to them. We shall not answer concerning these, as if the "type" or the "cube" or any other thing were more fitting than all others to be opposed by necessity. That which arises from a "moist substance," which is indefinite, is like a certain opposition. Thus, some define how there can be an opposite; for it is not only in substance that things happen to us in this way. But also, regarding the acceptance of the **definitive solution** <note>likely referring to the resolution of a logical problem</note> of the opposite among natural things, he himself declares this: nothing is opposite to substance. 

For this reason, in the present case and by itself, **air** is said to be among the opposites. Just as in natural philosophy he says certain things and particular things have opposites, he does not need to declare anything after this. Because in the **Categories** <note>Aristotle's treatise on the classification of predicates</note> he says substance is opposite to nothing, while in the works on physics <note>natural philosophy</note> there would not be an opposition of themselves. He makes use of the names of opposition for the antithesis of opposites. So then, it was necessary for substance, just as with the granting of honor. 

For indeed, as **Plotinus** <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD)</note> himself said, and as it has been stated in the **Sources** <note>Greek: *Pēgais* - likely referring to the "Chaldaean Oracles" or a specific Neoplatonic source text</note>, the fact that it receives opposites is not hinted at by the substance itself, but by that which is toward nothing in reality. As has been said concerning the "irrational"; and that "good" is held concerning "evil," but in every way the "other" is not a subsistence after the opposition. For in this way, the things after those are noted, as many as are not observed in opposition; otherwise, the definition will appear through the principles of opposition, as in the case of other things. For it does not exist in a **subject** <term>hypokeimenon - the underlying thing in which properties inhere</term> for both opposites to exist. Nor indeed in the "how."

# On Substance and Contraries

For the individual man under consideration, and the "animal" predicated of him, what kind of definition is provided? These things are set in opposition when taken as moving in contrary ways; or perhaps, lest we fall into suspicion regarding our needs, they immediately refer to a single body—that which has been mentioned—and those things which, by virtue of their <unclear>habitation</unclear> or position, are capable of receiving contraries. For each thing, whether <unclear>external</unclear> or concerning <unclear>lesser</unclear> matters, is either base or excellent in relation to bodies and their slowest movements. Nor is it only the case that it alone accepts changes into contraries, but it is also <unclear>opposed</unclear> to many others.

To those who say these things, a denial of all of them is necessary; for the species <note>original: "εἴδη" (eide) - the specific forms or types</note> and the genera <note>original: "γένη" (gene) - the broader classifications</note> of substances are not themselves among the things impossible [to receive contraries] as they exist in subjects, even if it <unclear>happens</unclear> that they cease to possess contraries in turn. Rather, if something is well-regarded in others, it exists in those others. But because it is observed that being a man is contrary [to something else] by way of accident <note>original: "συμβεβηκὸς" (symbebekos) - a non-essential property or "accident" in Aristotelian logic</note>, he distinguishes it otherwise through incapacity and action.

In these cases, while the substance <term>Substance (Ousia): the fundamental reality or "being" of a thing that stands under its attributes.</term> is one and the same—for example, **Socrates**—it is by nature capable of receiving contraries. Thus, the question arises: does the same man become ill and healthy? When contraries are observed, they will not be [present] at the same time, but in turn, even though Socrates remains in the same <unclear>place</unclear>. But it is not from such things that this happens. For an action <note>original: "πρᾶξις" (praxis)</note>, such as **sitting** or **standing**, may be base; for example, "walking tomorrow." At the same time, the state <note>original: "ἕξις" (hexis) - a stable disposition or habit</note> and the action may be one excellent and the other base. It is no longer a matter of the excellent and the base being one and the same.

There will be a simultaneous change among the contraries; it is similar to how an atomic substance <note>original: "ἀτόμῳ οὐσίᾳ" - an indivisible or individual substance</note> undergoes this change of contraries. For just as I carry these things which are always the same in relation to one another, and there was no necessity [for them to be otherwise], so it is also concerning their corruption. For example, a state might be great and terrible in its being taken away, yet it is never for the sake of being something else in this way. Or again, "walking tomorrow," the name of "thinking," and the "soul"—not even in this way will "walking tomorrow" exist. For life lived in such a way belongs to a perished action, or exists contrariwise; and having washed away what is present, there is no sweet thing, nor any action. For in this way, the action endures.

# On Substance and its Attributes

If it is taken away, it is no longer strictly called **substance** <note>original: *ousia*; the fundamental "being" or "essence" of a thing</note>, as is clear from the <unclear>singular</unclear> substances of the many. These things are also evident to us. If indeed the term "substance" introduces a cause for those things changing into it. But concerning the man, at one time he is healthy, and at another he is sick. This would be better: so that all things are a certain **accident** <note>original: *symbebekos*; a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like being tan or sitting down</note> in such a **category**. 

It is worth noting the unique property of substance: it is not an accident, but exists *in itself* <note>original: *kath’ hauto*; essential existence rather than existing as a property of something else</note>. And there is nothing else. It is also worthy to consider that substance possesses the capacity for change within itself. But that man [exists] in the whole of what is moved as a causative element, so that being one and the same, he always stands in the same way. For we would not say there is a contradiction in sight when he is the same, yet at another time he is sick and will not receive [health]. For he appears to move between opposites. 

Come now to the matter of imperishable beings; they do not participate in these two states, so to speak. To achieve so much as to make someone find a method of entry. Nor do they participate at all. <unclear>What kind</unclear> of things do I say will not be moved? If nothing else approaches, whether present or not, to look at it in this way; if not as it was according to its substance. It does not participate in opposites while spending time treading in a carriage, as is necessary. If, on the other hand, it receives any of the opposites, what is the benefit? But it is not *insofar as it is substance* that it is any of the opposites. 

The nature of substance has the quality of not having a "from where." But he himself is in the act of making that which is becoming. On the other hand, it does not have the capacity to participate in substance, but rather in external things. For example, "whiteness" or that which becomes a "shape," and not in the sense of being a **quality** <note>original: *poiotes*</note>. Fluidity is not a substance. But it is an innate property present in it. And if it accepts fluidity as if it were itself—for it is not by a quality, or by force, not at all. For it co-exists with the substance itself. 

Therefore, **quality** in circular motion is a necessity. And the **essential** <note>original: *ousiodes*</note> is not without a share of the substance within it. Whether one might say an "essential quality" is its own peculiar characteristic; rather, they are **essential differences** <note>original: *ousiodeis diaphoras*; the specific characteristics that define a species within a genus</note> and are complementary to the substance. Thus, the categories of substance stand firm, containing all things. For example, the members of a natural body must be inseparable within it, both of those judged later and those judged earlier. 

But let us behold everything again under another category. If the movements of **quantities** <note>original: *poson*</note> belong to every quantity, it is not possible for quantities to admit any opposites, but rather qualities. Just as things derived from quality are established, so neither **habits** <note>original: *hexeis*; stable dispositions</note> nor **dispositions** <note>original: *diatheseis*; temporary states</note> nor movements in themselves contain opposites; rather, it is the things produced that are opposites. We say, therefore, that to substance, everything [belongs] with power...

# On Affections and Qualities

...temperance <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosyne) — often translated as moderation or self-control</note>. We have spoken of **affections** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe) — refers to passive states, emotions, or qualities that can change</note> by the common definition to which they belong. Thus, if one says that a **statement** <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) — here meaning a proposition or sentence</note> is said to be "affected" by contraries, this is because it is capable of receiving the **true** and the **false** through a change. However, they are not named by virtue of the fact that they themselves undergo an affection. For by the fact that the things themselves change into contraries, the statement—which previously completed its role—what did it say? It is expected that the **will** <note>or intent</note> should run through everything in the arguments, just as **opinion** <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa)</note> runs through the true and the false.

But it does not "suffer" or undergo an affection in its nature. To be an opinion is to be true or false; and opinions are in harmony or out of harmony because of the **facts** <note>original: "πράγματα" (pragmata) — the actual state of affairs in the world</note>, but it is also said of the change itself. Just as a change occurs in the facts themselves, so too we do not say that the statement or the opinion changes; and this is so for the parts. Thus, one might call the statement or the opinion <gloss>or the opinion</gloss> "affections" in the sense that some **alteration** <term>alteration: "ἀλλοίωσις" (alloiosis) — a specific type of change involving quality rather than quantity or place</term> happens to occur. While things are altered and moved in the changes of facts, the opinion is simply "held" differently at different times.

Just as with the statement, as a statement it would never itself undergo such changes—those which involve truths and falsehoods. However, these are not the same as "affections." For they would be unmoved. But let us handle the matters of the will by the fact that it is so "peculiar" to it; yet it is so peculiar to the **essence** <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia) — the fundamental being or substance</note>. For it moves as much as the changes of the essences... such a change of it is an affection. For if previously the change was in something else, to have the opinion and that in which there is not only a **habit** <note>original: "ἕξιν" (hexin) — a stable disposition</note>. And if indeed in **atomic substances** <note>referring to individual, indivisible entities</note> it is called an affection; and also of the opinion, not the thing opined...

Furthermore, it is a poor argument that it is said of another in this way. For the **accident** <term>accident: "συμβεβηκός" (symbebekos) — a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</term> is of another. But as a **genus**, it is something that completes the underlying subjects. And likewise for its own **underlying subject** <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon) — the substratum or thing in which qualities exist</note>. One might be at a loss, having defined it in relation to the cause, how much has been added. For he does not yet teach us to seek the **incorporeal essence** apart from bodies. Nor is it the same as the form being separated from its mixtures... but it is necessary to avoid making it **godless** <note>original: "ἄθεον" (atheon) — perhaps implying a purely materialistic view without a higher principle</note>. So that in the affections themselves it is not possible to give a single definition. Nor does he say to the world what is "sweet" or "bitter" for all of them. For it is derived from the underlying subjects, or it confuses its own affections; just as <gloss>being</gloss> mixtures are a root and a sketch. Therefore, the affections are not more...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of quantity, specifically contrasting continuous and discrete forms as they apply to the physical and mathematical world.</meta>

The continuous is demonstrated when it is not merely joined to something else, but rather where both parts touch at a common boundary. For just as all things converge toward the center, the center acts as a common boundary within themselves in specific locations, which I might say are defined and found from without; yet when one does not labor over each part, we are persuaded that the plane follows after **quantity** <term>poson: the category of "how much" or magnitude</term>. And while the continuous is called **magnitude** <term>megethos: spatial size or extension</term> in every division of magnitude, the discrete, in turn, is called **multitude** <term>plēthos: a collection of distinct units</term>. 

Because it is thus distinguished, the whole cosmos is viewed through the spirit in this way and is said to be stable and spherical, as if grown together with itself, and again continuous in relation to another. But regarding things in a multitude, they are viewed according to their own specific concept, with the exception of the sphere. For him, these things have been found within himself. And while the continuous is "touching"—for it is something close and resists without being pulled apart—that which belongs to multitude is not called "touching" in the same way, even if all things in a multitude do touch. Nor, again, is it spoken of as resisting in that manner. 

Both of these fall under the world of the straight:
- **Arithmetic** deals with multitude.
- **Geometry** deals with magnitude.

Thus, everyone who exists in the theoretical study of unchanging things has recognized that multitude is defined by the "One" itself, while magnitude is defined conventionally. For as the theory says, number is the quantity relative to number; for there exists a great depth common within them. These are the limits, so that even the idea of each has its own substance. Regarding such things and all others, it is clear how the continuous is divided; the logic never says there is more. For the continuous appears within itself. Rather, neither the discrete nor the continuous is "above" the other.

Thus, that which is according to affirmation <note>original: *kataphasis*</note> or negation <note>original: *apophasis*</note> was "prior" in this way by nature, both in terms of declaration and in terms of truth. These things, when taken up, might still be well-reasoned and understood just like the same genus, which universally considers that "prior" and "posterior" of theirs. Insofar as its own species and communion are concerned, one might dispute the species with those who act from impulse. But one does not suppose the principles <note>original: *archai*</note> it holds in this way to practice a proposition, yet they are declarations either by nature or by the fact that they say the same genus—as if looking toward its composition—is thus grasped and completed together; it is not possible to depart from the life within them.

For concerning these things, the discrete <note>original: *diorismenon* — often referring to mathematical quantity like number</note> does not co-exist upon the straight line; for neither in the case of things growing in division <note>original: *amphimeria*</note> according to these and those is the discrete "prior," as he provides the causal explanation for things in the body. Just as because of the negations and affirmations, it does not even hold toward these. And indeed, concerning the compositions, each person acts and does such things. If, therefore, I do not speak toward the things that are similar and indifferent, how is it possible for it to be otherwise?

# On Syllogisms

In our pursuit of knowledge regarding syllogisms <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises</note> and aiming for a clear delivery of them, we have deemed it beneficial to bring together the principles found in *On Interpretation* and the labors in the *Analytics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s logical treatises, the *De Interpretatione* and *Prior Analytics*</note>, or rather to bring them to mind. These are as follows:
the premise; and affirmation and negation; how many quantifiers there are; what a universal premise is; and what a particular one is; and what a term is; and how many subjects there are, and what a predicate is; what the minor premise is; and what the major <gloss>premise</gloss> is; and what a syllogism is; and what "predicated of all" means; and what "predicated of none" means; and what it is to be "in a whole," and what "as a whole" is; and concerning the conversion of premises. And what a figure is; and how many figures of syllogisms there are; and what the combination of premises is in each.
We must begin, therefore, from the first. A premise is a significant statement of affirmation or negation. An affirmation is the existence of something in relation to something else; for example, "every human is an animal." For "animal" exists in "human." A negation is the non-existence of something in relation to something else; for example, "no human is a horse." For "horse" is separated from "human." A term is that into which a premise is analyzed. For premises are analyzed into terms, such as that which is divided and that into which it is divided, being the terms in a syllogism. Likewise with the affirmation. For "human" is a term; and "animal" is again a term. From these being composed, the premise is formed. There are four quantifiers <term>quantifiers: words that specify the quantity of the subject, such as "all" or "some"</term>: All; None; Not all; Some.
Of these, two are universal: "All" and "None"; and two are particular: "Some" and "Not all." Again, two are affirmative: "All" and "Some"; and two are negative: "None" and "Not all." A universal premise is one that possesses one of the universal quantifiers; for example, "every human is an animal" or "no human is an eagle." A particular premise is one possessing the particular quantifiers; for example, "some human is literate" or "not every human is evil." These, then, are universal and particular premises when they include quantifiers. If it happens that the premises are indefinite—that is, not having "all" or "some" or "none" or "not all"—the one with an article is equivalent to a universal premise; for example, "the human is an animal" is equivalent to saying "every human is an animal." But the one without an article, such as "human," is equivalent to a particular; for example, "human is good." For by its power it means "some human," and is equivalent to saying "some human is good." A premise is composed of a subject and a predicate, for the first term of the premise...
