<meta>This page continues a technical discussion of Aristotelian logic, specifically focusing on the "Square of Opposition" and the rules of conversion (antistrophe) for different types of propositions.</meta>

Not all contradictions are true at the same time, and all contraries are flawed in that while one may be true and the other false, they never both hold true together. For example: *Every man is white*; and its contrary, *No man is white* <note>original: "πᾶς ἄνθρωπος οὐ λευκός ἐστιν" - literally "every man is not white," functioning here as the universal negative</note>. These two terms constitute the opposition. The underlying concept is that many things are available to us as universals <term>katholou: referring to a whole class, e.g., "all men"</term> in relation to other universals, both affirmatively and negatively. Yet a proposition may only have a particular <term>merikon: referring to some members of a class, e.g., "some men"</term> scope; this, then, is the simple contradiction. 

Whenever this contradiction occurs before the affirmative terms, one must maintain the same terms even if I perform this operation. Regarding the remaining terms, only those with a simultaneously true opposition are considered. When he says that contradiction performs a specific function for the universal "every," he means:
*   Universal Affirmative
*   Universal Negative
*   Particular Affirmative
*   Particular Negative

For the universal, there is negation, and for the other, there is conversion <term>antistrophe: the logical process of swapping the subject and predicate of a proposition</term>. For example: *No man is just*; by conversion, *No just being is a man*. The affirmative propositions behave similarly in opposition and with the same terms. If we perform this—for it is itself a negation—they are likewise true together. Only the particular terms undergo change, for the same subject is assumed. Then, in order to show <gloss>the "at some time"</gloss> that this is the case, he adds a "but."

For the universal affirmative, conversion is no longer back to itself, but rather toward the particular affirmative. Otherwise, it is nothing. For if only the first part remains guarded, we would not be able to maintain the unity. From the opposition itself, it will convert, and likewise it is true. For example, if I say *Every man is an animal*, I speak the truth. But if I place it under contradiction and say *Every animal is a man*, I do not speak the truth. For a horse is an animal but not a man; that is how it stands. 

Furthermore, if we wish to preserve the conversions of the opposition, we convert the universal affirmative from the particulars. For example: *Every man is an animal*; but [only] some animals are men. The particular affirmative, however, converts back to itself. This applies to the particular affirmation: for example, *Some student is diligent*; and *Some diligent person is a student*. This holds true together with the other properties of the opposition. 

The particular negative, however, no longer converts either to itself or to another. For if I say *Not every animal is a man*, I speak the truth. But if I say *Not every man is an animal*, it is a falsehood. And while these are necessary matters, the particular negative does not convert. Since these things are so, it [sometimes] converts [accidentally]. For example, if someone says *Not every man is white*, he speaks the truth. And if someone says *Not every white thing is a man*, he also speaks the truth. Thus, the contingent ones do not hold true, but the contradiction does. We speak of the contingent...

In this figure <note>The Third Figure of the syllogism, where the middle term is the subject of both premises</note>, the minor premise must be affirmative. If these conditions are met, a conclusion follows. In this figure, the conclusions are reached through **conversion** <note>original: "antistrophe" – the process of swapping the subject and predicate of a proposition</note>. Syllogisms are formed from each case because of the contradiction to the unguarded <note>unclear: likely referring to a term not "guarded" by a universal quantifier</note>. The contradiction is set to be affirmative. For those cases where it exists, there are syllogistic modes for every phase; therefore, these are also a safeguard for that figure.

There are, then, two primary modes of the figure. The first arrangement is that in which an affirmative premise leads to an affirmative conclusion. For example:
*   **Animal** is predicated of every **man**.
*   **Man** <note>original: "anos," a common scribal abbreviation for "anthropos"</note> is predicated of every **man**.
*   Therefore, **animal** is predicated of every **man**.

This was the conclusion. Analogously, it will be shown through conversion in the Third Figure. For since the conclusion is such—as **animal** is of every **man**—then **man** is of some **animal**. For "some" is used for the particular conversion. For underneath, **man** is of every **man**, and this **man** is of some **animal**; for when this is converted, **animal** is of some **man**. Thus, for all, it is persuaded by conversion, though it is itself unclear in the first figure.

The second mode is that which proceeds from a universal affirmative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise, resulting in a particular negative <note>The text here describes the mood Darapti, though the scribe's description of the conclusion as "particular negative" (apophantike) seems to be a slip of the pen or a specific variant, as Darapti usually yields a particular affirmative</note> conclusion. For example:
*   **Animal** is predicated of every **mule**.
*   **White** is predicated of every **mule**.
*   Therefore, **animal** is predicated of some **white** thing.

Converting this likewise: if **white** is of every **mule**, then every **mule** would not be <note>unclear: the logic here follows the rules for conversion</note> of some **white** thing. But since **animal** is of every **mule**, and **mule** is of some **white** thing, then **animal** is of some **white** thing. If the particular converts, it belongs to the first figure.

The third mode in this figure is from a universal affirmative major and a particular affirmative minor, resulting in a particular affirmative conclusion. For example:
*   **Animal** is predicated of every **man**.
*   **White** is predicated of some **man**.
*   Therefore, **animal** is predicated of some **white** thing.

Converting this into the first figure: if **white** is of some **man**, then converting it, as we say, **man** is of some **white** thing. Since **animal** is of every **man**, and **man** is of some **white** thing, the conclusion is: **animal** is of some **white** thing.

The fourth mode is from a universal negative major and a particular affirmative minor, resulting in a particular negative conclusion. For example:
*   **Animal** is predicated of no **stone**.
*   **White** is predicated of some **stone**.
*   Therefore, **animal** is not predicated of every **white** thing <note>i.e., "Animal is not of some white thing"</note>. It will be converted thus...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of space, time, and motion, specifically focusing on the definitions of continuity and the impossibility of indivisible parts forming a continuum. It aligns with the beginning of Book VI of Aristotle's Physics.</meta>

# On successive <gloss>13th</gloss> natural elements. Definitions of the 7th <gloss>book</gloss>. <note>The scribe likely refers to Book 6 of Aristotle's Physics; the "7th" or "13th" numbering may reflect a specific manuscript tradition or chapter division.</note>

Continuous things are those whose extremities are one. Touching things are those whose extremities are together. Successive things are those which have nothing of the same kind between them. "Prior" is that which is nearer to the motion, or that in which the motion is, or the source of the motion. That which is nearer to the motion is "prior," whether in terms of the "now" or in terms of time. But if they are divisible, the same reasoning holds. We state clearly then: every continuum is divisible into parts that are always divisible.

<meta>This page begins the famous 'Poimandres,' the first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum. It establishes the visionary encounter between the narrator and the divine Mind.</meta>

# The Poimandres of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ Τρισμεγίστου Ποιμάνδρης." Hermes Trismegistus, or "Thrice-Great Hermes," was a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of these sacred texts.</note>

**O**nce, when I began to meditate on the things that are, and my thoughts soared to great heights, my bodily senses were restrained—much like those weighed down by sleep due to an excess of food or physical exhaustion. It seemed to me that a being of immense, boundless magnitude called my name and said to me: "What do you wish to hear and behold? And what do you intend to learn and know by your understanding?" I replied, "But who are you?" "I," he said, "am the Poimandres <note>The name 'Poimandres' is often translated as 'Shepherd of Men,' though it may also derive from an Egyptian phrase meaning 'Mind of Ra.'</note>, the Mind of the absolute Sovereignty. I know what you desire, and I am with you everywhere." I said, "I wish to learn about the things that are, to understand their nature, and to know God. Oh, how I wish to hear!" He spoke to me again: "Keep in your mind all that you wish to learn, and I will teach you." Having said this, his form changed, and suddenly everything was opened to me in a moment. I saw a limitless vision: all things had become a sweet and joyous light, and I was filled with love as I gazed upon it. 

But after a little while, a downward-tending darkness arose in one part—fearful and gloomy, coiling in tortuous curves. I perceived the darkness changing into a certain watery nature, unspeakably agitated, giving off smoke as if from a fire, and producing a sort of mournful sound. Then an incomparable cry was uttered from it, sounding like the voice of fire. 

But a holy Word <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos). In this context, it refers to a divine, creative utterance or reason that brings order to chaos.</note> descended upon that nature, and a pure fire leaped forth from the watery nature, upward into the heights; it was light, piercing, and active all at once. The air, being light, followed the breath <note>original: "πνεύματι" (pneuma). This can mean breath, spirit, or moving air.</note>, ascending from the earth and water as far as the fire, so that it seemed to hang from it. The earth and the water remained mixed together by themselves, so that the earth could not be seen apart from the water; yet they were kept in motion because of the spiritual Word hovering over them within hearing. 

Then the Poimandres said to me: "Have you understood what this vision means?" "I shall know it," I said. He said: "That light is I, Mind, your God, who existed before the watery nature that appeared out of the darkness. And the luminous Word which comes from the Mind is the Son of God." "How is this?" I asked. "Know it this way: that which sees and hears within you is the Word of the Lord, but the Mind is God the Father. For they are not divided from one another; for their union is Life." "I thank you," I said. "Then perceive the light," he said, "and make yourself known to it." 

When he had said this, he looked me in the face for a long time, so that I trembled at his appearance. But when he looked up, I saw in my mind the light consisting of countless Powers, and a world without limits had come into being...

Motion is as if in a boundary. What kind of motion is to be grasped? That which turns before itself. And the revolution is the same as the motion around itself by means of station and rest. For that which is "around itself" is either motion or about itself; and it is moved because of being around itself. And from that which is around itself, thus the visible star is the counter-motion, by the motion itself and the turning one. For one must create a certain fabric of expression, like sentient living beings. For example, a sail in which the thing moved is seen; and while the water is carried along, it proceeds by resisting the water that strikes it; such things happen to all. These things are balanced and peaceful. It is most clear to the sight what kind of motion it is. For every motion is moved as a substance <note>original: *hypostasis*</note> within rest.

Therefore, the motion of the divine and everything in the material world does not happen to occur by the natural things of the cosmos, but by the things in the <note>likely "divine"</note> toward that which is according to nature. Either the multitude, or fire, or some other incorporeal thing <note>original: *asomatos*</note>. For it does not move that which is not obedient to bodies. But neither does the living being move the whole body as something soulless. How then is it nourished by motion? Therefore, the wooden thing as well as stones and all other things are in motion, for they do not partake in <unclear>incomprehensible</unclear> motion. For that which is inside the body, and the mover within it, does not move as motion moves. Both are the movers: that which is carried by the one carrying it. Which is motion and the state of being. For being from motion and purely, it is moved by nothing except that it is moved by a non-shaking motion. But the things moved are not moved in motion, and the things within them as a whole. That being [motion] and stretching out, the description of its moved part is clear, not incomprehensible. The essence <note>original: *ousia*</note> of beings is motion. Only that which is non-being is more than the appearance of essence. For the underlying void can never produce mortal things. It is not, therefore, in itself as motion, and in the same thing. Such as the whole cosmos. All the void. And the whole entirety. And all the most numerous things within it. A saying concerning...

## The Sacred Discourse of Hermes

The glory of all things is God and the Divine. And divine nature is the beginning of existing things—God, and Mind, and Nature, and Matter. Wisdom is for the manifestation of all that exists. The beginning is the Divine, and Nature, and Activity, and Necessity, and the End, and Renewal. For there was boundless darkness in the abyss, and water, and a subtle, intelligent spirit, existing by divine power in Chaos. All was without form and without quality, but fire was kindled from the light [out of] Chaos. And all things, and there as from nature, as if from fire. Therefore, as things were defined and reconstructed, all the light things were distinguished [and rose] to the height, and the heavy things were founded upon moist sand, being separated by fire and <unclear>suspended</unclear>, to be carried by the spirit. And as it was seen, how they were moved by those things easily moved. And there were the gods seen in the stars, with all their signs. And [the cosmos] was articulated together with the gods in it. And for the fire to encompass the air in a circle, being observed in the spirit, every living thing [was formed]. And every earthly thing shall move through the divine power, which obeys their will. And to move all the wild beasts, and all things, and the birds, and the creatures of the water, and all things, and every seed of growth, and grass and—

And this very Mind he sent down; having filled a great mixing bowl <note>original: "krater" — a large vessel used in ancient Greece for mixing wine and water; here it symbolizes a font of spiritual essence</note> with it, he dispatched a herald. And he commanded the herald to proclaim to the hearts of men: "Dip yourself, you who are able, into this mixing bowl. Do so in the hope that you shall ascend to Him who sent the bowl down." If anyone understands these earthly patterns—those, therefore, who understood the proclamation and were baptized <note>The term "baptized" here refers to a spiritual immersion in Mind/Intellect rather than a physical water rite</note> in the Mind, these people partook of Knowledge <note>original: "gnosis" — experiential spiritual knowledge</note> and became perfect human beings, having received the Mind. 

But as for those who failed to heed the proclamation, these possess the power of speech <note>original: "logikoi" — possessing 'logos' or reason, but here used to distinguish those with mere logic from those with higher 'Mind'</note> but not the Mind; they remain ignorant of why they were created and by whom. Their sensations are very similar to those of irrational animals; their temperament is composed of passion and anger, and they do not marvel at the things worthy of contemplation. Instead, they devote themselves to the pleasures and appetites of the body, and because of these things, they believe that man was made for this fleeting age. 

But those who have partaken of the gift from God, these, O Tat, are immortal rather than mortal when compared by their works. They have embraced all things in their own Mind: the things on earth, the things in heaven, and whatever exists above these. Having raised themselves to such a height, they beheld the Good. And having seen it, they considered their stay here on earth to be a misfortune. Having looked down upon all things, 
<margin>71</margin> both corporeal and incorporeal, they hasten toward the One and Only. This, O Tat, is the science of the Mind: the abundance of divine things and the contemplation of God. 

"And I too, O Father, wish to be baptized." 

"Unless you first hate your body, O child, you cannot love yourself. But having loved yourself, you shall possess Mind; and possessing the Mind, you shall also partake of the science." 

"How do you say this, O Father?" 

"Because it is impossible, O child, to be occupied with both: with things mortal and things divine. For since there are two kinds of things—bodies and the incorporeal—in which the mortal and the divine reside, the choice of one is left to him who wishes to choose. For it is not possible to choose both; and where the choice is left, the preference for one diminishes the energy of the other. The choice of the better not only turns out to be the most beautiful for the one who chooses, having deified the man, but it also demonstrates piety toward God. But the choice of the lesser destroys the man, even if it commits no offense against God other than this: that just as processions pass through the middle of the way, unable to achieve anything themselves yet obstructing others, in the same way..."

This is "becoming"; this is what happens after the beginning. The Monad, therefore, insofar as it contains every number, is contained by all; and all number exists, not being exceeded, it belongs to number. But everything that comes into being is imperfect, and indivisible, and subject to increase and decrease. But to the Perfect, none of these things happen. And that which is capable of growth increases from the Monad; from a composition toward the Monad. Nor do they count the Monad as being separated. This, therefore, is the All and the One, and all things would become toward the One; and since the One is in the thinking, because by the eyes of the heart, my child, you will find no small faith. That which is through the Mind <term>Nous: divine intellect or intuitive perception</term>; after it, the art journeys. For it held the straightforward idea. And once in the depth a prayer; and in the height according to the appearing, you are near to the paths.

->First, concerning the Name.<-

Consider how that which seems invisible to the many might become most manifest to you. For it would not exist at all if it were truly invisible. For everything that appears is <term>begotten</term> <note>Greek: genneton; referring to things brought into existence or created</note>, for it has been made manifest. But the Invisible always exists, for He has no need to be made manifest; He exists eternally. He makes all other things manifest while remaining invisible Himself, as He is eternal. While He reveals all things, He is not Himself revealed; He is not brought into being, yet in our <term>imagination</term> <note>Greek: phantasia; here meaning the faculty of mental representation</note> He presents all things. For imagination belongs only to those things that are begotten; indeed, imagination is nothing other than the process of becoming.

It is clear, then, that the One who is unbegotten is also beyond imagination and remains invisible. Yet, by giving form to all things, He appears through all things and in all things—especially to those whom He wishes to reveal Himself. Therefore, my son Tat, pray first to the Lord and Father, the Only One and not merely "one," but the source from whom the One comes, so that you may be enabled to perceive so great a God. Pray that at least one ray of His light may shine into your <term>intellect</term> <note>Greek: dianoia; the faculty of thought or understanding</note>. For <term>contemplation</term> <note>Greek: noesis; direct spiritual perception</note> alone sees the invisible, as it is itself invisible.
<margin>—</margin>
If you are able, Tat, He will appear to the eyes of your mind. For the Lord is not begrudging; He reveals Himself throughout the entire universe. Strive to perceive Him, to grasp Him with your very hands, and to gaze upon the image of God. But if even that which is within you is invisible to you, how shall He, being within Himself, appear to you through your physical eyes?

If you wish to "see" Him, contemplate the Sun; contemplate the course of the Moon; contemplate the order of the stars. Who is it that maintains this order? For every boundary is defined by limits and measures. The Sun is the greatest god of the heavenly gods, to whom all the other celestial gods yield as if to a king and a mighty ruler. And yet this great being, larger than the earth and the sea, submits to his station, having stars smaller than himself revolving around him. Whom does he respect, or whom does he fear, my child? Each of these stars does not travel an identical or equal path. Who is it that has defined the manner and the magnitude of the course for each? Consider the Great Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major</note>, which turns around itself and carries the whole cosmos with it. Who is it that possesses this instrument? Who is it that set the boundaries for the sea? Who is it that established the earth?

For there is indeed, O Tat, a Maker and Master of all these things. It is impossible for place, number, or measure to be maintained without a Creator. All order is impossible <unclear>to be</unclear> created in a random or immeasurable way; no, not even this order, my son, could exist without a guide.

# That the greatest evil among men is ignorance concerning God.

If the All <note>The Universe or Totality</note> always exists and is a living being, and a body does not exist otherwise, how could a <unclear>living being</unclear> within that very body be destroyed? For the World <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos)</note> is, for us, immortal, both in its limit and in its life. And the World is under the All. For Eternity <note>original: "αἰών" (aion)</note> is not destroyed as Eternity, nor is it destroyed within the World. For Eternity is the instrument of the World. And as for changes, men call them certain weaknesses of death in the World, leading to the destruction of all things. And if the parts in the World were destroyed, the World would be destroyed. But God is first, and the World is a living being. For first of all, truly eternal and unbegotten, is God, the Creator <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiurgos)</note> of all things. Second is the one made by Him according to His image, sustained and nourished and made immortal by Him, as a living immortal being by its own father. For the "immortal" differs from the "ever-existing." For the one has been brought into being by another. And if it is by Him, by whom all things <unclear>were made</unclear> <margin>35</margin> it was made, yet it is unbegotten. For the "eternal" is not the same as the "All," nor does it follow from itself. But the World was generated by the Father as eternal and immortal. And as much as there is of the World's own material—and this is the All—the Father had created it by giving it substance, under a summit of forms. This, then, is the first thing encompassing substance, and of all things it is the immortal and powerful eternity of fluidity.

# Of Hermes Trismegistus
## The enigmatic discourse to his son Tat, the title of which is: The Key:

<margin>11</margin>
Yesterday’s discourse, O Tat, I dedicated to Asclepius. But it is necessary to deliver the present one now, so that it may also receive its proper conclusion. Therefore, O Tat, God and Father and the Good are the same thing. Or rather, they are an energy <note>Greek: *energeia*, meaning active power or operation</note>. For that which belongs to nature and growth is, so to speak, a motion; but not a motion of the will in the same place. And yet there is a motion of such a kind that the universe is filled by it. This exists within the realm of the will. For while energy belongs to another, one must not marvel at this energy itself in any other way, but speak of it and believe in it. For to do otherwise would be impious. For the pious thing is to hear all things with piety and silence, not only that all things exist. For reverence belongs to the Father. But the energy of all things is not from them, but for the sake of those things that are. For that which truly is, belongs to the Father. For the essence of being the Good is to exist for nothing else but for another. This is what the Sun alone among the gods in the cosmos does, not in place of being, but being itself the Good. Nor is it that which is through him. But that which is the right of the suns. For they do not even live. But God the Father and the Good certainly receive existence. And the Good is that which is also power. For without this we cannot even perceive the things that are. For it is the cause of the things that are moved and the things of nourishment. But see for one who has received it, the judging sign of the sun. For the Good has come as nothing else. But the Good cannot be elsewhere, but must be in God, 
<margin>112</margin>
by necessity, or rather necessity alone; and that God is never to be grasped by one who is, for everything is either that which possesses reason. For one must not, O Tat, do anything. For the Father takes up a very great deal of time in such a child. And where the Father and the Good are, they are together. For the things pertaining to the vision of the soul are in clear perception. But God and Father and the Good, by being all things, are thus good and are better than the gods. For they have no end. and all things around him are less. For every opposing thing is in the same place for all. For it cannot be seen, but it is known. But the Good is in God. These things fill the engine of the soul like fire from all knowledge. And one would perceive nothing, if the Mind were the eye, under the divine energy. Eternity <note>original: "αἰὼν" (Aion) - refers to the personified concept of eternal time or the divine realm</note> is not by chance. What kind of things are they? All other things are to be learned accurately. And the All is one. Not of salvations and beautiful things, except for those that are necessary. So great a length is this cause of the cause itself. ## Mind to Hermes: This discourse is concerning a defined essence of the soul and a contrived counsel. So be it.

As indeed each living being comes from the world. From many things come many of the things that differ among all, and from the God of all things. For it is a small thing among men. But to one who understands, it will be found <margin>42</margin> more clearly. For I would trust you alone through this revelation. Time is in Eternity, and Eternity is in the All. And Eternity [is also there]. The world is in Eternity. But when it is substituted, Eternity is in the world. The world is in Time. Time is in becoming <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis) - the process of coming into being or generation</note>. Just as the essence of God is the Good, the Beautiful, Happiness, and Wisdom; so the essence of Eternity is Sameness. The essence of the world is Order. The essence of Time is Change. The essence of becoming is life and death. The activity of God is Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> and Soul. The activity of Eternity is permanence and immortality. The activity of the world is restoration and counter-restoration. The activity of Time is increase and decrease. The activity of becoming is quality. Whatever things are Eternity, they are in God. Whatever things are the world, they are in Eternity. Whatever things are Time, they are in the world. And becoming is in Time. And while Eternity stands still around God, the world moves within Eternity. Time is limited within the world. Becoming happens within Time. Therefore, God is the source of all things. Eternity is the essence. Matter is the world. Eternity is the power of God. The world is the work of Eternity, having never been born and yet always being born by Eternity. Therefore, it shall never be destroyed. For Eternity is indestructible. Nor shall anything in the world perish, for the world is contained by Eternity. And what is the wisdom of God? The Good, the Beautiful, Happiness, all Virtue, and Eternity. Therefore, Eternity adorns immortality and permanence within itself. Eternity [adorns] matter. For that matter, being in a state of rest, is mastered by Eternity. In a certain way, Eternity also rises up. For motion and time, in this way, also preserve Eternity itself. It is <margin>43</margin> as if eternal and indestructible. In these things, change is wisdom. And the essence of Eternity is Sameness. The essence of the world is Eternity. [The essence] of change [is time]. And God is in the Mind. The Mind is in the Soul. The Soul is in Matter.

All these things are not disconnected. For all things are the body of the Mind <note>original: "Νοῦς" (Nous) — the divine intellect or cosmic consciousness</note>, in which all bodies exist.

Fortune is full of the Mind and of God; if indeed he himself fills it. And if all these heavens are also fulfillers; if indeed the great God himself and the master of all things were to have become all things in this way; if indeed all things are living beings. And if anyone should be so divided within him in that identity; for even the things on the earth are included, about which this discourse is concerned along with the others. Eternity <note>original: "αἰών" (Aion) — the personification of eternal time and the divine realm</note> holds this together; for since this moves either Providence <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia)</note> or Nature <note>original: "φύσις" (physis)</note>. And beauty does not exist unless it is a kind of inhabited world, and in the earth are all the things that belong to the earth. And the things existing in the earth are living beings, and it could not be otherwise; or else the eternal things and the same things and those concerning other things do not exist. For never in any way do the things in the midst of others come to be; this must be admitted in accordance with the whole truth. For the like is not similar to the unlike, even if it is something unique. And certainly not to any other of those things of the composition of days. For all things are unique. 

The soul is immortal and the change is toward the mind; or else he will not make it anything other than himself. For God is not to be grasped by virtue; if all the lands were to be all things; for she would not dare this. But neither was there disorder anywhere in the cosmos <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos) — the ordered universe</note>; nor in anything else; <margin>44</margin> for "shameful" is a new name. 

We know this well from the things that come to pass; for God calls all things to become. And these things proceed according to the Mind; for the one who acts is in all things, not equal to any greater thing. Nor is he lacking in anything. But he is all things; for by the power of his activity, he has become the underlying substance for them. But I also become all things; and when I saw the cosmos reflecting him—whoever he may be—I saw his beauty pure from that source; no body was defiled; nothing was older; but all was completely flourishing and young. 

And indeed, it is more fated; you know also why all things remain in the cosmos in their varied forms; and the opposites; and the different things are fulfilled by Eternity. All things flee being full; there is a void nowhere; for the friendship and the union of opposites and of unlikes always flee, even as the world is ordered by the power of God into his manifold generations. His works do not cease at the beginnings and ends of the cosmos; for the work is not merely an object of thought; it is the instrument of all nature, transforming the matter of all things. By these diminishments of the whole, he cares for all things as they are established in the cosmos by the nourishment and age of the ethers. The Father <note>original: "γενήτωρ" (genetor) — the progenitor or creator</note> is the same in the multitude of the immortals and of all the gods; and in the middle of both, the immortals and the mortals, the moon is circumscribed; and all things are full of soul <note>original: "ψυχή" (psyche)</note>.

# On the Divine Powers and the Cosmos

Into these same powers, as many as are proclaimed by both, into the realm of sensible things <note>The "sensible" refers to the physical world perceivable by the senses, as opposed to the intelligible or spiritual world.</note>. And indeed, from the extremities into the mind. The mind belongs to them. And these things belong to the humble part of the entire body; some things, therefore, it possesses. For we might possess the likely traits of living bodies and of the changes as they are separated into one another, from the unutterable resurrection of the whole. But in the other things (not even into the whole of the body), number belongs; for without number, no constitution or system will move for the sake of each of them. Every cause is masterly, a number begotten and imperishable. Having perished as a sign, then, the cause is as it might receive it. And the height. This entire world, which is fire and possesses individual Words, so that it is not motionless and with the perception of the whole, the universe is the fullness <note>original: "pleroma" — a technical term for the totality of divine powers</note> of life. And there is nothing in this throughout the whole that is motionless in the face of eternal change. Neither of the whole, nor of the parts. For it lives. For nothing conquers it. Nor is the whole in such a state. It is not begotten in an orderly fashion.

Nor indeed is the <term>First Cause</term> <note>original: "πρῶτον αἴτιον" - the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic thought</note> merely beautiful. He alone is truly wise, containing all things within himself, full and most ancient. For the beginning of all generated things comes from the first principles. There is, however, a distinction among the <term>intelligible entities</term> <note>original: "νοητῶν" - things grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> and in the continuity of their creation. The Form was modeled as something immaterial, yet of no physical image. For there is a scattering so that it might run back toward the One. Of these things, looking upon the invisible is a peculiar, wondrous, and <term>theurgic</term> <note>original: "θεουργούμενον" - referring to divine work or ritual that connects the human to the divine</note> act.

It is both marvelous and blessed that the First is known. For spiritual things are more ancient, while sensible things come later and cease to be known. For the contemplation of beings, remaining one, does not rest. But the contemplation of the First is that of the things in relation to ourselves. Therein lies <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "δυνάμει"</note> and, in its essence, <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν"</note>. Everything exists for the sake of the Good. For the difference between the intelligibles is a power, but actuality consists in all things coming into being. Therefore, the rest from this creative governance is called its "use." The beautiful thing that has come into being approaches it.

For this alone is nothing, nor is it a "circumcision" <note>likely used here in a metaphorical sense of "cutting off" or "separation"</note>. Every intelligible is entirely according to
<margin>48</margin> the intelligible letters and gods; everything that has come into being is full of the clarity of vision. It participates in a certain way; it participates with all things. It is among the changeable things, or rather, it is the benevolent. For it is not just "any" thing, but movement and wisdom. And it shone forth from within, as much as is always possible. For one cannot separate the First, but that which has come into being must necessarily exist. For it exists in relation to itself and belongs to itself. Therefore, those internal things could not be permitted to cease from one another.

Inasmuch as he creates, he is nothing other than the First alone. It is necessary for him to be simple to all. For he must be himself in such a way as to be directed toward the First, which is below <note>This may refer to the emanation descending to lower levels of reality</note>. Everything that has come into being is unable to have been brought into being by itself. Being brought into being by another, it must necessarily be generated. Since the First exists, the generated thing thus comes to be in this manner. For since the "Other" is infinite, he modeled the nature of the Form. There is, therefore, the Other. But the First does not exist by the laws of that which is becoming. Let it be that the image is like [the original], this being made to endure. That which is primary is what it is, but the generated thing receives it, whatever it may be. These things especially [show] the variety of generated things, by their tribes, out of fear in their <term>substantial reality</term> <note>original: "ὑποστάσει"</note>. To exist forever comes from the First. For it is as it seems. The First is everything; and that which is toward the divine is as if to be.

# Hypothesis <note>original: "ὑπόθησις" - the premise or subject of the argument</note>

In this way, his [work] is necessary; both in the change; and in the whole, this is a thing that experiences; but in the other, it is not a molding in this way; but such as are also innumerable. For how are all things necessary? And God Himself; in the union in which one sees the "In" <note>referring to the mystical or essential indwelling</note>. :-

<meta>This page begins a technical treatise on logic, specifically focusing on hypothetical syllogisms. The text follows the Aristotelian and Stoic traditions of formal reasoning.</meta>

# By the most blessed, wisest, and most learned <unclear>concerning hypothetical</unclear> syllogisms.

The so-called hypothetical syllogisms consist of two premises, each partaking of the hypothetical nature. From the first premise comes the consequence and the members. For example: *If it is a human, it is also an animal. But it is indeed a human; therefore, it is an animal.* 

The first part is called the **antecedent** <note>original: "ἡγούμενον" (hegoumenon) - the 'leading' part of a conditional statement</note>, and the second part is the **consequent** <note>original: "ἑπόμενον" (hepomenon) - the 'following' part</note>. This type of reasoning, which functions through position and consequence, is called **connective** <term>connective: (συναπτικόν/synaptikon) a conditional "if-then" statement</term>. The term that is taken up in the second premise is called the **substitution** <note>original: "μεταλήψις" (metalepsis)</note> or the substitutive. Then, the word "therefore" introduces the conclusion. Often, both the antecedent and the consequent are negated—to speak more generally—for otherwise, no conclusion is reached.

Of these hypothetical arguments, if they happen to be **undemonstrated** <note>original: "ἀναπόδεικτοι" (anapodeiktoi) - basic logical forms that are accepted as self-evidently valid without further proof</note> syllogisms, they are as follows: the inferences are drawn according to consequence, from which their names and such conclusions are derived, forming this specific method. 

The first type of connective syllogism results in the consequent. For example: *If it is a human, it is also an animal. But it is indeed a human; therefore, it is an animal.* Behold, by the **positing** <note>affirming</note> of the antecedent, the consequent was established. And by the positing of the consequent, its own property follows—which would be <unclear>absurd</unclear> <note>The author likely refers to the fallacy of affirming the consequent</note>. 

The second type <unclear>regarding the modes</unclear> occurs by the **removal** <note>negation</note> of the consequent, which removes the antecedent. For example: *If it is a human, it is also an animal. But it is not an animal; therefore, it is not a human.* Behold, by the removal of the consequent, the second type likewise removes the antecedent. This is also called the **conversion** <term>conversion: (ἀντιστροφή/antistrophe) here referring to the logical law of contraposition</term>. Thus are the arguments according to consequence from the antecedent.

All these are taken up in the introductory lessons, either by their concepts or as they fall into one another. And since in <unclear>connective</unclear> arguments the **middle term** <term>middle term: (μέσον/meson) the term that links the subjects of the premises</term> is held or is indefinite. That which is held as a consequence is the middle term, which others also use. For the middle is something belonging to it. The first is living, as it is the lesser. Indefinite are the one and the middle, as in the rule of the middle. Often there are also things **between** them, such as gray, <unclear>late</unclear>, irrational, and similar things. Hence the hypothetical syllogism is so named by seeking the assumption of a middle term from the immediate terms. 

It is taken from those that fall into one another; once found, the middle term is inferred. That which is based on the middle is the more "reputable" <note>likely referring to 'endoxa' or generally accepted premises</note> from the remainder or from those based on a hypothesis. To speak of reputable things again, the consequent is inferred. For example, as in the case of one's own opposites, which is an opinion—the opinion and that which is upon it. But if he is worthy, then he is not <unclear>a human</unclear>. Behold, by the positing of the one, the other is gone; the remainder is removed in relation to the consequent. Having been found impossible, holding the middle term, such as...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical structures, specifically focusing on the "undemonstrated" or indemonstrable syllogisms used in Stoic and Peripatetic logic to define relationships of equality, difference, and contradiction.</meta>

Through the affirmative, we establish the lesser. But indeed, that which is neither greater nor lesser is established as equal. By the position <note>original: "θέσει" - the formal setting down of a premise</note> of one, we achieve the negation of the others. 

Regarding what is the greater and the lesser: again, by the negation of the others, the equal is established in this way. The equal is that which is established as being neither greater nor lesser. But indeed, it is neither greater nor lesser; therefore, it is equal. Observe how, by the negation of the others, the resulting tension <note>original: "τὸ τεῖνον" - likely referring to the logical force or "tonos" in Stoic thought</note> is brought together, and this too is a labor <note>original: "πονὸς"</note> of how things are substituted for one another. 

However, the third mode of the indemonstrable <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A syllogism is a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> is not like this. It is not by the <term>governing faculty</term> <note>original: "ἡγεμονικοῦ" - the Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul/mind</note> alone, from which is taken the removal of the greater or lesser from their own parts. And through these, they form the syllogism by the combination of the negation. 

For example: if a horse is either white or black. But indeed, it is white; therefore, it is not black. For by the choice of the one, the other is negated. This does not change for anyone or anything. For example: a horse is either white or black. Often the attribute <note>original: "συμβεβηκός" - an accidental property</note> is considered, but as we said, it is with a combination of the negation. That is to say: it is not both white and black. And by the position of the one, the rest is negated. 

In the same way, this also applies to conditionals <note>original: "συνημμένων" - connected or hypothetical propositions</note>. For in this way, it is a horse. For example, so that if the first is true, the second is also true. But indeed, it is a human; therefore, it is not a horse. And here, likewise, it occurs through the combination of the negation. For thus it is joined: either the first is something, and it is both a horse and a human. For it often happens to them that it is a horse and is not a human. 

Thus, we have reflected on the third mode. For instance, the ancients make this the third mode. Nothing is lacking in taking the wholes from the positions and the genus. Having a name as many as they say the "all" is. As if to say that, if she dedicated <note>original: "ἀναθεῖσα" - possibly a corruption or specific logical example involving an offering</note>. And having dedicated three, the world is eternal. Either the world is eternal, or the whole world and the souls are. Or the whole world and the souls will rest in a conclusion, and the souls are doubted. For in this way, they do not have the properties of the subjects. Therefore, the conclusions <note>original: "ἄρας" - literally 'takings' or 'inferences'</note> are again under the genus according to every cause. 

Thus, all the demonstrative syllogisms are called <term>indemonstrable</term> <note>original: "ἀναπόδεικτοι" - basic logical axioms that are so self-evident they do not require proof themselves.</note>. Therefore, the principles of such things are entirely agreed upon. 

These are the matters concerning the indemonstrables.

As the **first mode** <note>original: "πρῶτος τόπος" - the first of the indemonstrable syllogisms in Stoic logic</note> is gathered: when they posit the antecedent <note>the 'if' part of a conditional statement</note> as being connected. 

The **second mode** is that in which, by the removal <note>original: "ἀναίρεσις" - the denial or negation</note> of the consequent <note>the 'then' part of a statement</note>, the antecedent is also removed; this is also called "sequence" or "by connection" <note>original: "συναφεια" - a logical binding</note>. 

The **third mode** is that found in the connection of a negation. 

The **fourth mode** is called a **yoke** <note>original: "ζεῦγμα" - often referring to a disjunctive syllogism (either/or)</note>; because the removal of one of the remaining parts results in the composition <note>original: "σύνθεσις"</note> of all the rest; this mode is also taken from immediate opposites and is shown in problems that possess a middle term. 

The **fifth mode** is the converse of this: because by the positing of one, it removes the remaining part or parts.

# Natural Problems of Alexander of Aphrodisias

<margin>The cause of graying hair</margin>
Why do the hairs of men become gray? It is because graying usually begins in this area <note>referring to the temples or the front of the head</note>. The parts toward the forehead of the head are more susceptible to diseases and are more phlegmatic <term>phlegmatic: containing an excess of phlegm, one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture</term>. The solution lies in the temperament <note>the balance of humors</note>. The cause in the front of the head is the <unclear>lightness of spirit</unclear>; for which reason the hairs there are soft and sparse. Of those hairs that are curled, their nature is to be sealed by dryness. Among hairs, those from the <unclear>gate</unclear> are not found according to their length, as in the case of 
<margin>The cause of baldness</margin>
southern parts which are drier and denser. This is why people go bald, as observations show it results from dryness. For this reason, those with curly hair, being dry-headed, go bald more quickly. However, they turn gray more slowly, as the dryness overcomes the phlegmatic deposits. They say also that those who suffer from insomnia <unclear>among others</unclear> [experience this]. For it is not only by dryness; just as many infants, being moist and full of breath <term>pneuma: the vital spirit or breath of life</term>, also experience these occurrences. And the moist conditions, such as those who have blistered or used frequent baths, happen to be less affected by the <unclear>seeds</unclear> of the spirits—I mean the nose, the mouth, the ears, and the eyes. But those with straight hair, being naturally "under-headed" <note>perhaps meaning having a moist brain or lower heat</note>, suffer the opposite. Therefore, they turn gray more slowly, as they do not go bald at all. People also go bald due to hereditary diseases; for like an inheritance and other ailments, these are innate conditions, as are the things we drink. Snowy [hairs] become gray, and they possess less sensation and spirit. The cause is often mucus. The change in the color comes from the phlegm that is produced. Sometimes the hairs happen to be golden-colored, whenever either white or yellow bile is mixed with the phlegmatic humors. At any rate, those who are <unclear>...</unclear> and sleepless are causes [of this]. Being situated in the body, they happen to be colder and become like parched cheeses. And they suffer less from many <unclear>collected</unclear> deposits in the pores. They are dried out by those who have natural <unclear>seals</unclear>. And because of this, they are sleepless. For infants are moist in their pores and their seals. And being entirely moist and full of breath, they change often. Because they are moist and generally so; however, phlegm is moist and cold. Otherwise, the <unclear>bregma</unclear> <note>the top of the head</note> of the head is blood-like, and consequently, the occurrences are most diverse.

Why are eunuchs for the most part crooked-footed <note>original: "στραβόποδες" (strabopodes); referring to a bowing or twisting of the legs</note>? Therefore, as the legs carry the weight of the body held upon them, they become distorted. In this way, they are bent by the weight, just like a cylinder. Thus, eunuchs are both womanly and weak. They also become addicted to wine and are babblers, as they are lacking in will. For having become cold, they seek the opposite for themselves; and wine is hot by nature. But those who are mostly drier are curly-haired, fair-skinned, muscular, and stronger for work.

And why are they high-voiced <note>original: "ὀξύφωνοι" (oxyphonoi); literally 'sharp-voiced'</note>? We all know it is due to the weakness in their thickened necks; being weak, and providing more space for the breath, it makes the voice high-pitched. Because of these factors, they exist as men who do not <unclear>speak/sound</unclear> like men.

### Why those who are afraid are pale

For the sake of safety, (it draws together with its great flame, it uses its own nourishment and a little blood, the skin becoming pale and chilled).

For those who control the passages of the spirits, now having become weak, the parts are lifted up. And being held by the spirit, they jump up against the weight of the psychic power.

I say that the stomach is situated right against the windpipe <note>original: *tracheia artēria*</note>. They hear poorly in the chest <note>original: *thōraka*</note>. Again, when their breath does not pass through and the fullness is depicted, they feel the pain.

### Why do those who are struck see fire?
Because the whole visual body <note>the eye and its internal fluids</note>, being thinned by the blow, is suddenly set on fire. And just as in the air, such a thing appears as darkness and at night. For in this way, by reasonings or by pieces of iron being rubbed against each other, the air being struck and thinned out—from which a reflection is damaged—becomes intense fire. Likewise also with anchors. 

### Why do all stones send up fire when rubbed together?
Because of the necessary force and [being] light. And for those carrying sand. For it is not for me that the air, being slapped, is struck. And being struck intensely and stretched out, it is destroyed. And it appears also that in the mountains you remain together with all things; it is struck and set on fire. Such are some of the things being rubbed. 

The fire produced from the sun and water comes about when the solar rays of the sun, shining against the glass of the mirrors, are set on fire even more. And again, through the emission [of light] by receiving it. 

### Why is the downward reclining more [effective] than the upward?
Because we have the intense spirit in a straight downward reclining. For in this way the stone, being vibrated, has a downward motion, but in the upward vibration of the <term>sigalis</term> <note>likely a corruption of a technical term for a spark or a specific mechanical part</note>, we are not able to [lift] the weight toward the top. For in this way the stone being thrown [produces] this fire and it [goes] upward. For this is heavy and downward-tending. 

### Why do infants cry and sprinkle [tears] when they are born?
Because the breath <margin>-</margin> [gives] sensation and to a soul being hosted in a strange place. From the belly indeed with the body and from the womb, into the air perhaps or outside. Perhaps it is by the light and the [rays]. For it is not likely that the voices [cry] because they are about to see some chaos; that body seems [to suffer] and because of this the infants cry in it.

# On the Causes of Fevers

It is clear, then, that when we observe the beginning of the causes, the various elements of <term>sympathy</term> <note>The Greek *sympatheia* refers to the interconnectedness of body parts where one organ affects another.</note> no longer all run together for them, nor are they carried along all at once or in the same manner. <unclear>Bees</unclear> <note>The reading is difficult; it may refer to a metaphor for swarming humors.</unclear> of the <unclear>choroid</unclear> <note>Likely referring to the choroid plexus or membranes in the body.</note> someone cries out, commanded from the straight line; but as many things as cease below and approach the image in the middle, while another greater part gives way, even the opposites; and thus it occurs with the filling of the light itself. When it appears, that which has the name "marshy" arises from the midst, creating differences in diseases according to the target of the locations. For the <term>humor</term> <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> within is variegated, which is why **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> says and calls it "many-colored." Whatever the needs of the whole, it is but a small and short-lived thing; for it was destined to be so, because of the fire. But those things that are chaff-like and moist quickly become a smoky fire—see the fire—and the result of the burning is slow. For when the **yellow bile** <note>original: "xanthē cholē"</note> is about to putrefy in the large vessels—I mean the **veins** and **arteries**—and they do not happen to find a way out, it results in a longer duration because it is in a place where the <unclear>fever</unclear> endures for the longest time, as in the case of a **burning fever** <note>original: "kausou" - a high, acute fever.</note>.

But if the flame should not happen to putrefy in the small veins and arteries near the skin, the mixture is small and long-lasting, a wandering state as in the case of a **semitertian fever** <note>original: "hemitritaiou" - a fever recurring on a specific cycle, often associated with malaria.</note>. For the rest, these things have a war that is easily won; since when the yellow bile putrefies in the small vessels, the mixture produces a <unclear>fever</unclear>, but one of short duration, for the fire there is as if long-lasting.

# On Sound, Laughter, and the Senses

The sounds in the air and in the earth are analogous to motion; for first, there is that which occurs in the passage <note>original: "πόρῳ" - a pore or channel</note> in a circle. Every motion of theirs is not slightly affected by the "tortoise" <note>likely a reference to the resonance chamber of a lyre or a specific mechanical shell</note> and the changes of the water and that which is in the earth. From the investigations of the ebbs and flows concerning the passage according to the depth: the water recedes again, so that it moves in a circle. And this happens during a state of rest, until the stillness is extinguished. But the things occurring according to the tension of a stone <note>referring to the ripples or vibrations caused by a stone thrown into water</note> necessarily make the inner circle and the outer circle a sweet task to behold; for because of this, the blow from the stone in no way divides the impact upon the water.

### Why is laughter produced with many tones?
Laughter occurs from the exhalation; for they say it flows in all at once from the internal organs, and along with the breaths come the laughable things, like a sort of reflux. But indeed, by nature, I say that strange things also happen, and the spleen is not the cause <note>The author disputes the common ancient Greek belief that the spleen was the seat of laughter</note>. 

The cause is a violent, foreign motion toward the grime and the **melancholic humor** <term>Melancholic humor: Black bile, one of the four bodily fluids believed to govern temperament and health</term>. And thus, while the blood itself might be preserved, it feeds upon the base as if by nature and by humor. But the humor in wine cheers these people and brings about good spirits instead; yet never when it is agitated. 

### Why do offspring not occur?
Because the sensitivity of animals is easily affected, as is the purity of reports and the precision of the voice. Let there not be anything before the breaths in the spirit <note>original: "πνεύματι" - pneuma, the vital breath or spirit</note> and the contraction of the appearance of the tongue. It leaves one being **melancholic** for the rest, causing the color of the surface to vanish, and it arises from certain other bright things. Especially at the extremity, it is a bold need; and reasonably, the voice proceeding from it carries either reputation or sensitivity.

### Why are those deaf from birth also mute?
Because of the motion, they hear nothing in return, and they do not speak with a voice. Regarding those who are hunchbacked, they say that between the humps there is a star <note>This may be a corruption in the transcription or a specific anatomical metaphor</note>, and those who have an idle tongue also share this cause. However, they are not entirely deaf, nor entirely mute; for the breath alone stops the acoustic sense. Similarly, the stooped and others are not deaf from birth. The slurring of the tongue in the hunchbacked comes from the passage of the tongue. 

### Why do many of the elderly become deaf?
Because of the slowness of their nourishment, being idle, they accumulate an abundant humor. After meals, therefore, this flows—as is now demonstrated by the forms and the **melancholy**, or the secondary effects—following sleep.

# On Natural Effluxes and the Afflictions of the Body

The flowing droughts <note>original: "αύχματα" - refers to periods of extreme dryness or parched conditions</note> are by no means caused solely by the heat of the earth. Regarding other afflictions, some occur due to the skin <note>original: "δορήματος" - likely referring to the hide or outer covering</note> and originate from the depths; or they are an efflux <note>original: "απόρροια" - a flowing out of particles, a common concept in ancient physics</note> that flies upward, arising from both the matter and the sheer quantity of the substance. Others occur by force, happening through great intensity and strength; flowing in many ways toward the center, they similarly fail one another. 

Furthermore, if tears were to flow in this manner, plagues <note>original: "λοιμοί"</note> are shut out by the dense efflux, acting like the gods of life over these sufferings. In children, the channels <note>original: "σωλήνες" - anatomical ducts or vessels</note> around these parts rise up, either because they drink much or are intoxicated by underlying vapors. For that part is more unrestrained, and being weak, it cannot contain the pouring matter. 

Again, a gangrene <note>original: "γάγγραινα"</note> of rheum <note>original: "ληματιωδών" - referring to eye-mucus or discharge</note> occurs in our young children. Among children, some are unspeakable; it happens to whomever it chances, making them weak and inferior, for many of their stumbles are due to the age they have reached. 

### On Sleep and Motion

Furthermore, it is proposed that a palpitation <note>original: "παλμόν"</note> resulting from motion produces sleep. Since the gate of nobility is in the light of touch, from these very things a sovereign motion arises, moving upward toward our head, leading to our own strength and sleep. Some say that a breath in the hope of touch, along with the highest parts, moves through the vein; this is the vital motion of the prosodies <note>original: "προσωδών" - perhaps referring to the rhythmic pulsations or tones of the body</note>. The things that happen toward this motion and the palpitation—due to the upward-sending of the nerves—reach the head, and thus we act more frequently.

### On the Moon and Eclipses

Again, things become worse with the moon; the moon and darkness belong to the eclipses <note>original: "ελλιπτικών"</note>. This is because the moon, at the proper time, reaches the boundaries of the ecliptic nodes. When these are moved, an effect arises from the shadow of the earth, because the sun is larger. Because of the lines reclining from the moon, a well-flowing motion continues toward certain impulses that fall upon them. But the sun is affected only by the ecliptic nodes under the shadow of the same moon, as if it were in labor. From this come their downfalls. 

In those things which test it, some are hidden according to the reversal of the disks, and it is not the moon. But it says that he suffers more continuously. When the moon moves, all the eyes <note>original: "οφθαλμοί"</note> <margin>catchword: eyes</margin> are affected. Inasmuch as they deliver us from the demons <note>original: "δαιμόνων" - here likely referring to malevolent spirits or supernatural influences on health</note>; for the luminaries <note>original: "φωστήρες" - the sun and moon</note> send forth through the void a violent efflux, ridding us of the base demons.

# On the Soul and the Spirit

This [relationship] also applies to the soul in respect to the spirit <note>original: "pneuma"</note>. That it happens to belong to bodies is a view held by everyone, including [the ancients] themselves. Since there is a lack of <unclear>this</unclear> which is <unclear>most sensitive</unclear> and for this reason the most extreme, he says that in this way a body is always present to the soul in some identical manner. This spirit, when it suffers poorly—as in the case of grief and other things—does not function rightly. It brings about a dulling of the memory and becomes thickened, whereas when it becomes the opposite, it provides the memory with vigorous activities and orderly arrangements toward first principles. # On the Digestion and Health of Children

Therefore, regarding the causes <note>original: "αἰτιαις"</note>, neither the quantity nor the quality of food is the cause of illness in children. At the same time, in the **belly** <note>original: "κοιλίᾳ" - used here to mean the stomach or intestinal tract</note>, the small amount is dried out along with the urine; or, according to natural principles, those who have produced a great deal of drink in the bellies again produce the matter of urine. Because of this, **diarrheas** <note>original: "διαρροίαι"</note> appear when the body has become weak. So that which nourishes is taken up along with the gruel. The nature of the **evacuations** <note>original: "ὑποχωρήσεων" - bowel movements</note> happens in the case of those who exercise much, and in those unaccustomed to it, or from wherever the things consumed are slowly and with difficulty sent to the belly. Both **sweet** and **salty** flavors are the most **purgative** <note>original: "διαχωρητικώτατοι" - promoting the passage of waste</note>.

For it is in the [vessels]. Other flavors have a salty quality or are corrupted in the belly.

But that which is honey-like becomes heavy and is introduced more among the troublesome things. Both **whey** <note>original: "ὀρρὸς"</note> and [other fluids] loosen the belly. But **wine** <note>original: "οἶνος"</note>, when drunk in large quantities, does not only do this. For these things are not without substance.

Why it is that [the pig] has long since stood apart. Why are the sexual impulses <note>original: "ἀφροδίσια" (aphrodisia)</note> of the goat more [frequent] than those of the sheep? Is it because, as with men, as much as any old [habit] of the belly? Of the sow, the parts are in the belly.

Why does the wild sow give birth only once, while the domestic ones give birth twice? Is it because the domestic one is [reared] on prepared nourishment and [gives] a cry once? **Why** does [the pig] rejoice in foul-smelling things? Is it because it has a wide and swollen snout? And it was possible for everything to be moved according to every smell. Why do the tusks grow? Whether as some [remedies], the halves coincide; they grow without being equal, just as in the others...

# † The Handbook of the Great Teacher Alcinous
## On the Doctrines of Plato. The Definition of Philosophy.

The following would be a teaching of the most important doctrines of Plato.

<margin>What is philosophy?</margin>
**P**hilosophy is the longing for wisdom, or the release and turning around of the soul from the body, as we turn toward the objects of the intellect <note>Greek: noēta; things understood by the mind rather than the senses</note> and those things which truly exist. Wisdom is the science of things divine and human.

<margin>Who is the philosopher?</margin>
**T**he philosopher is the one named after philosophy, just as the musician is named after music. It is necessary for the philosopher to be naturally disposed,

<margin>
How and in what
manner must the
philosopher
be instructed in
the elements.
</margin>
firstly, toward those studies which are able to bring him close to and lead him toward the knowledge of essence <note>Greek: ousia; the fundamental reality of a thing</note>, and which do not wander according to the realm of becoming <note>the physical world of change</note>. Secondly, he must have a passionate love for the truth and in no way embrace falsehood. In addition to these, he must be naturally temperate; and regarding the emotional part of the soul, he must be naturally composed. For he who devotes himself to studies because he wishes to understand the things that exist and looks toward this goal, would not practice the pursuit of pleasures. Thus, the one who intends to practice philosophy must be self-controlled in his judgment. For pleasure is contrary to the rational soul. He must also be high-minded in his thoughts and care for nothing small (for it is reasonable that he be naturally inclined toward heavenly things, toward the divine, and toward temperance). He should also possess a readiness to learn and a good memory; for these qualities are indeed similar to the virtues of the philosopher. These natures, if they receive the proper and correct education, appear to result in a perfect man; but if neglected, they become the causes of great evils. Plato addressed these qualities by the same names as the virtues: such as courage, temperance, intelligence <note>Greek: synesis</note>, and justice.

<margin>What is contemplation?</margin>
**S**ince life is of two kinds, the contemplative <note>Greek: theōrētikos</note> and the practical, the main point of the contemplative life lies in the knowledge of truth; while that of the practical life lies in the performance of those things dictated by reason. The contemplative life is therefore honorable, but the practical life must also be accepted as necessary. That this is so, one may learn from the following.

<keywords>Alcinous, Plato, definition of philosophy, wisdom, contemplative life, practical life, virtues, temperance, essence, Middle Platonism</keywords>

If, therefore, contemplation <note>original: "theoria" (θεωρία) — the act of looking at or observing truth</note> is the activity of the mind, then those who think are coming into being. But action <note>original: "praxis" (πρᾶξις) — practical or moral conduct</note> is the settled state of the rational soul accompanied by a certain foresight. The rhythmic harmony of nature and the order of life is the law of life, and this is in every way most perfect. And that which precedes it is named practical wisdom <note>original: "phronesis" (φρόνησις) — ethical intelligence or prudence</note>; which, through its formation, becomes a likeness to the divine. Hence it is also called "that which leads." It is this which brings us near and offers us the goodwill of God. And not only toward Him. There are more beautiful and higher callings; and indeed that which is called "that which does not yield to us."

For while action exists for the sake of the practical, the essence of living according to the law exists for its own sake. It is beautiful, being a cause through causes and actions, which are among the things done for the sake of living well, which are seen in the present time, along with the particular characters of men. But insofar as nothing else is needed for living well, unless practical wisdom should build a form toward the knowledge of them. And in this respect, contemplation is this active beauty. Toward the best foundation, just as among evils if these things lead the way, they establish for you a perfect mastery of language. And they do so reasonably. It must be said of the things within our power <margin>not</margin> to the philosopher, that he must by no means fall short of contemplation. But also of <margin>the</margin> practical things themselves. For he is trustworthy in practical matters through the philosopher himself according to Plato, in those things where the builders are. Both in the knowledge of beings and in knowledge itself, just as beauty exists in action, so it exists in the contemplation of reason itself. And indeed, this knowledge of existing things is called "theoretical." But that which is in the practical realm is "practical."

That which concerns reason is "dialectical." It divides itself either into the defining part and the definitive; and the demonstrative; and the syllogistic. This latter is divided into the demonstrative, which concerns the true syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>; and into the "entrepreneurial" <note>original: "epicheirematic" (ἐπιχειρηματικόν) — a dialectical argument based on probable premises</note>, which concerns the reputable or likely syllogism; and into the "eristic" <note>original: "eristikon" (ἐριστικόν) — a contentious or hair-splitting argument</note>, which concerns the false syllogism, which is called an incomplete syllogism. And the following suggestions are set forth: that while [contemplation] is primarily proper to the philosopher, it is also necessary.

Practical matters concern character, and the theoretical concerns the forms of character.

### Concerning the Criterion

Every judgment involves that which is judged, and of necessity, that which arises from the choice present in the act of judging. And indeed, in this way, there is a judgment which is therefore the <term>criterion</term> <note>original: "kriterion"; a standard or instrument for judging truth</note>. And the manner of the judging is the "judge." That which is judged is like the honey <note>a classic philosophical example: the object being perceived</note>; that which judges is the "judge," such as the person who says the honey is sweet. The criterion is like the natural organ of judgment. Its primary purpose is to grasp the truth and distinguish it from falsehoods. This is nothing other than natural <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational faculty</note>. To speak more clearly, the judge is the philosopher. That by which the judgment is made is the criterion, and the reason through which the truth is judged is also the instrument by which we say it is guided. Some speak of reason as being entirely true and secure. These things are secure for all matters. Of these, the first is God, who is clear. The second follows, and the third is as it is. These concern both the intelligible and the sensible: one concerns beings and is of a <term>scientific</term> <note>original: "epistemonikos"; relating to certain, demonstrable knowledge</note> form. The <unclear>divine</unclear> reason concerns sensible things, and is both sensible and a matter of opinion. The scientific reason possesses certainty and stability, inasmuch as it deals with certain and stable principles. But the persuasive and opinion-based reason is multifaceted, because it does not deal with stable things, but rather through those things which...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical discussion on the faculties of the soul, specifically focusing on the distinction between intellectual perception, scientific reasoning, and sensory experience.</meta>

Intellectually, then, it exists in this way within the body, and at that point one must speak of intellection <note>original: "noesis" — the act of the mind grasping a truth directly</note> and the innate concept <note>original: "emphyton ennoia" — an idea we are born with</note>; intellection being that which will exist in the soul’s underlying subject. We do not say that scientific reasoning <note>original: "epistemonikos logos" — logical, demonstrative proof</note> is the origin of all forms of knowledge—at least not of those we are currently discussing—but rather that it is the capacity of the soul to be separated. Or as we do not say, yet it is certainly known according to such a clear natural concept. And this belongs to the natural concept, and the simple form is one thing. A mixture of each of these, and of imitations. Since, therefore, the majority are signs, scientific reasoning is not a matter of mere conventions. He says it exists in an underlying subject.
<margin>Sensory intellection is intellection combined with sensation; the one directed toward sensible objects is uniform.</margin>
**O**n the one hand, then, there is truly both scientific reasoning and the opinions of some, which he compares, as well as sensations, so that even the parts fall under them; for instance, speaking of 
sensible things. And from the intelligible things, the primary ones are those that exist and are. 
The secondary ones, on the other hand, are those already in matter—the communications of matter that are inseparable, specifically to the soul. Of the primary things: those already within them. Since there are as many sensible things as there are, of the primary ones there are qualities; for example, color or whiteness. Then there are the accidental properties; for example, "the white thing"—by which we know this collection has been colored, such as a fist <note>likely used here as an example of a "collection" of parts forming a whole</note>, and in this way also sensations. 
One kind, then, belongs to the primary things; it is called primary. The other belongs to the secondary things and is called secondary.
<margin>Concerning which, right reason judges the practical matters falling under art.</margin>
