<margin>On what subject and how Plato used syllogisms</margin>
Universal categorical <note>original: "kategorikoi" – a direct statement of fact, e.g., "All A is B"</note> syllogisms are the simple ones; for example, "everything just is beautiful." Hypothetical ones are those that show a sequence or a connection <note>original: "akolouthian" – logical consequence, often "if... then" statements</note>. Plato made use of the study of syllogisms; he also used the specific types themselves, for he conducts his inquiries through them. However, he does not primarily use their technical names; though it is a worthy syllogism, he calls it a "reasoning" <note>original: "logos"</note>; in which, when certain things are laid down, something other than what is set down follows. Of syllogisms, some are categorical; others are mixed hypothetical; and these are the mixed ones. In categorical ones, both the premises <note>original: "lemmata"</note> and the conclusion are simple propositions. Hypothetical ones are those consisting of

<margin>On what subject and how Plato used syllogisms in his own works</margin>
hypothetical propositions. Mixed ones are those composed of both. He used them—some through propositions, in which he addresses our thoughts, such as this one; and this one in which he addresses the sophists <note>Professional teachers in Ancient Greece often accused of using fallacious reasoning</note> and the wicked; and the definitive ones against the equally-matched sophists; for example, he speaks of a "link" and a "horse." Of the categorical syllogisms, there are three figures <note>original: "schemata" – the patterns of logical argument</note> according to the first type, in which the middle term <note>original: "koinos horos" – the shared term that links the two premises</note> is the subject of one and the predicate of the other; the second, in which the middle term is the predicate of both; and the third, in which the middle term is the subject of both. Terms <note>original: "horoi"</note> are the parts of the propositions; for example, "man is an animal"; we call "man" a term, and "animal" as well.
And the so-called first figure—Plato actually uses it in many discourses; for example, "the other" and the manner in which he acts. Also the so-called "superior" type, for example in the *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of man and justice</note>: "just things are beautiful; beautiful things are good; therefore, just things are good"; and the former is as if toward the greater. Thus he converses in the *Parmenides* <note>A challenging Platonic dialogue on the nature of "The One"</note>: "The One has neither corners nor a circumference; but things participating in a shape exist because of them; therefore, the One, not participating in these, does not participate in a shape." And the third figure is used thus in the *Parmenides*: "The One, however, in terms of shape, is according to the third figure; that which participates in shape is affected by it; therefore the 'More' <note>or 'The Greater'</note> is affected by it." Therefore, in comparisons in many books, we liken the book to the things that exist. The greatest use of the second figure, however, is in the arguments regarding number. For he says there is neither beginning, nor middle, nor end. For he says the middle is not some things in this way and some in that, nor those at the beginning. Since it has no beginning, it does not participate in shape. Therefore...

Since we are always accustomed, in the knowledge of names <note>original: "onomatike gnosei" — the study of how things are named</note>, to transition from visible and sensible things to those that are more obscure to us, it is necessary to proceed toward the naming of this method. This method was discovered <unclear>without being taught</unclear> by the ancients, but was first treated as a formal theory by those before us. **F**or I said that it is understood in two ways: the geometrical and the arithmetical. And those who set out from these call it **analytical** <note>term: analytical — a method of "working backward" from a conclusion to find the necessary principles or starting points</note>. Just as proofs are composed from the top down starting from first principles, so too is the form from which we compose; yet no one in practice uses anything greater than what occurs according to our own nature. But this is not merely some <margin>dialectic</margin> <note>term: dialectic — the highest form of philosophical inquiry through dialogue and logic</note>; they named this mathematically. **A**nd the dialectical method is the method used by us in mathematical progress; this performs the primary service, not being subject to matter, but existing in its own nature. Hence, it is fitting for dialectic to be a "form." We say that it differs from neither moving nor seeing, and we call it, with certainty, "analytical." For we do not refer the proofs back to their proper principles by mere potentiality. Rather, they say that the "form" of the first things is the opinion of bodies; they might also lead mathematical study back as "image-like," viewing it as an image of the things above. Since dialectic is the strongest of the mathematical sciences, it is necessary that the testing of it becomes immovable and that the study be made unsurpassable. For just as guards are placed for horses, so guards are placed <margin>concerning principles</margin> for the rest. **A**fter these things, we shall recall the first principles, and simultaneously treat the theorems of the higher, deceased first principles in a theological manner. Let us therefore consider the causes of these, looking at the parts of bodies. Having concluded with the gods themselves and nature, let us consider <margin>concerning matter</margin> while speaking about matter. **I**n matter itself, therefore, there must be something incorporeal which produces qualities and colorings. Thus, every thing is both bodily and intellectual. But that which is lacking in reason possessed such a property that it receives all generation; for our rational accounts come from that which contains the form within them. And it is necessary for us to consider this very form as something immovable, without its own idea, and existing as something shapeless. Having been discovered, it was named in this way properly, and it is likely to be a certain endurance in parts. And being a rhomboid of shape in everything, it has no shape of its own.

Being nothing other than [themselves], even bodies [are such]. For bodies are subject to passions and are in a state of flux, and they are never in the same state or remaining the same. <margin>That the creative power of beings is incorporeal.</margin>

In the same way that a single seal produces many impressions <note>A classic Platonic metaphor: the "Form" is the seal, and material objects are the wax impressions.</note>; and likewise these things come from the myriad of myriads of numbers. How then is it not likely that this power is august and superior to them—such as power and necessity itself? And the world, being the most beautiful handiwork, was made by God the Craftsman <term>Demiurge: the divine artisan who shapes the material world according to eternal forms</term> for all, since he also brought the essence of the world into the best possible state. For he himself, by the necessity of their natures, bound them together with a bond, so that it might be modeled after what was laid up [in the heavens]. 

He did this for the sake of assimilation, as far as possible, to the Living-Thing-Itself <note>original: "autozōon" (αὐτοζώου). There are traces [of the forms] which possess the potentiality of the arrangement of the elements. # On Geometric Symmetry and the World-Soul

The underlying principle possesses a symmetry with a right angle <note>original: "γωνίαν ὀρθὴν"</note>. One part is two-thirds. Regarding the symmetries of this, the same fourth part, loosely, is the scalene triangle <note>A triangle with three unequal sides</note> of the **pyramid**, the **octahedron**, and the **icosahedron**, serving as their element. The **pyramid** is composed of four equilateral triangles, which themselves would be formed from four of the aforementioned scalene triangles within the pyramid. The **octahedron** is composed of eight; similarly, the **icosahedron** consists of twenty <note>The Greek text says "κἐ" (25), but contextually refers to the 20 faces of the icosahedron</note>. From these scalenes, the **dodecahedron** is also composed, formed of hexagonal rhombi <note>original: "ἑξαγώνων ῥομβομέτρων"; likely referring to the division of pentagonal faces</note>, a shape brought together in that construction. For from the isosceles triangles (since he deems all right angles to be good), the **cube** is composed of four.

As for the **dodecahedron**, he made use of it for the whole <note>The universe</note>, which was invisible. Because it appears impossible for a living being <note>original: "ζῷον"</note> to be constituted from the aforementioned elements, it is handed down as having sixty parts in total. Thus, everything coming to the dodecahedron, each of its 12 existing faces is divided into five such parts. Consequently, there is a necessity for them to be made of triangles. In the whole **dodecahedron**, there is a composition of three hundred and sixty triangles, which happens to be the same number as the degrees in the **zodiac** <note>original: "ζωδιακῷ"</note>.

Through this, a natural union is imprinted upon **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη"</note>, and we shall be moved further by the previous inclination of these parts. For indeed, it came into being in various aspects, fitting them all together in proportions <note>original: "ἀναλογίαις"</note> to one another. Not even these, however, were separated or set apart. Remaining behind, they provide a certain seed to matter. Therefore, as the revolution of the cosmos is tightened, it is carried along. And being driven together, all the fine-grained parts reach toward one another, into the spaces of the coarser-grained parts. Because of this, nothing is left behind as a void, empty of body.

There is also a symmetry of proportions in the composition of the **soul** <note>original: "ψυχῆς"</note>. Matter is brought together under the ruling principles and is moved by them. Both, therefore, even down to the participation of the remnants, are governed by the powers of those things which are circular in their motion. For the sake of this, I judge the others by their order; every beginning of all existing things depends on which order is within it, so that there may always be a natural relaxation for those things that fall under it. And though greed disturbs it, it remains in harmony with the whole and with the body of the living being in its proper order. For saying that there is an immaterial living being of the intelligible realm, he established that the bodies themselves exist by participation in it. Appearing...

# On the Nature of Man and the Cosmos

The parts of matter <note>original: "ὕλης" (hylē) — the raw physical substance of the universe</note> themselves, at appointed times, as if they were to be given back in exchange for themselves, would be able to do so without contribution. Every primary human nature, as they were thus composed, possesses these things of wisdom for all and for the recording peoples; all those things of the human race. Indeed, the souls are of the nature of God, because the Creator <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiourgos) — the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</note> of the whole made them equal in number to the stars. Having placed each soul into the universe as if into a carriage <gloss>nature</gloss>, he told them the laws of destiny, legislating first so that he might be blameless. He showed that sufferings would be tripped up within the body: first, sensation; and upon these, pleasure and pain, fear and anger. Those who master these will live justly, and those mastered by them, unjustly. And because each living being would arrive at a state of perception, it shall be guarded by sensation; and how it happens in the whole when they recognize that it comes to be. For those things that do not cease, but are forever perishing in their nature through the things kept for them—some coming to be, some perishing, and others being required to hold their essence.

Behold, the gods fashioned what was poured around men; from fire and earth and water. Borrowing certain portions for this path, they joined them together with invisible bolts, making not one world of the same parts, so that each might fill this body, being one, yet to be set free. Just as a field of plants is illuminated, so is the whole upon the entirety, and the organs of sensation; they attempted to surpass what was fitting. And they heard of things not numbered toward the dissolution and release of the triangles <note>Plato's theory that the four elements are composed of geometric triangles</note>. From these, we know the generation of the quantity of which the body was composed. As for the bone, such is the nature of their flesh, dipped in white water and fire. The trees, from which we also derive our whole being. This very flesh of man is a composition along with the juice, as if of something fermented. A coil thereafter, divided from its source.

# On Flavors

**On flavors.** Having concluded our discussion of odors, it is worthy to note that while odor is considered a more refined substance, flavor possesses a much thicker consistency. Odor is said to exist within vapors; for odor arises from a spirituous emission <note>original: πνεῦμα (pneuma) - often referring to a gaseous or vital breath</note> of both air and water through their mutual interaction. Yet, flavor shares a commonality with both air and water. Indeed, for each of these, flavor is also present. For the perception of these things arises from the same source as the sense of smell is constituted.

The varieties of flavors are numerous, just as odors are; their affinities and differences are perceived by our presence. It seems that odors serve as the criteria <note>or "judges"</note> for flavors. These are compared and distinguished according to the transformations of the flavors. In defining the species of simpler flavors, there are differences such as:
*   **Sweet**
*   **Sour**
*   **Harsh** <note>original: στρυφνὸς (stryphnos) - often used for the astringency of unripe fruit</note>
*   **Austere** <note>original: αὐστηρὸς (austeros) - a dry, rough flavor like certain wines</note>
*   **Salty**
*   **Pungent** <note>original: δριμὺς (drimys) - sharp or piercing to the senses</note>
*   **Bitter**

Among these, the sweet, even if it possesses a natural quality, occurs in all other things. As for the flavors, some belong to those things possessing an excess of moisture. They say that in relation to the sweet ones, there are the sour ones; while the hard ones are produced, as well as those in the middle, such as the pungent. They define the pungent as that which possesses a vehement and intense quality, much like the bitter. The pungent quality cleanses the areas around the whole with salty elements.

In a similar way to the sweet, and among those that exceed in roughness, is the harsh. That which is similar to the sour is the austere. From these, the power <note>term: δύναμις (dynamis) - the inherent capacity or medicinal property of a substance</note> inherent in flavors is constructed. In terms of perception, some are cold, others are hot, some are hard, and others are light or heavy. Therefore, one must judge the matters concerning flavors and the differences within them. They would say nothing else than that the primary elements utilize the <unclear>foam</unclear>; and the sense organs are analogous to this, which always occurs in relation to the foundations of the sense of smell.

<summary>This text explores the Aristotelian classification of flavors (sweet, sour, bitter, etc.) and their physical relationship to moisture and odors. It categorizes flavors by their sensory "powers" such as heat, cold, and astringency.</summary>

<keywords>flavors, odors, Aristotle, sensory perception, sweet, bitter, pungent, astringent, moisture, pneuma</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ideal governance, transitioning from the character of the ruler to the specific classification of political constitutions, heavily drawing upon Platonic and Aristotelian political theory.</meta>

# On the Nature of Rulers and the Forms of Government

What kind of leaders philosophers must be: they must be contemplative regarding **the Good**. For only in this way can the same individuals who have hungered to see the truth also manage the affairs of the wicked. For such forms <note>referring to the ideal archetypes of governance</note> are not first encountered as riddles by chance; rather, it is when philosophers become kings—or when those now called "robber-kings" become true philosophers by a divine fate. For the best and most just constitution (as one might say) is the most beautiful when it is self-governing in each city. Just as there are guardians who are rulers by nature, and defenders who are allies by nature, so too should this system be constructed.

In this regard, there are three primary types:
1. **Aristocracy**, when the best men rule.
2. **Timocracy**, where the rulers are motivated by honor <note>from the Greek 'timē' meaning honor or price</note>.
3. **Oligarchy**, the rule of the few.

And after these, **Democracy**, which establishes itself; and finally **Tyranny**, which is the worst of all. This triad <note>likely referring to the first three positive forms</note> is to be preferred because it results in an orderly or humble state <gloss>and it is a thing of the most upright likeness.</gloss>

One must be wary of innovations introduced into the laws. For the laws should be practiced with clear definitions. If this reasoning holds, there must be a certain "most beautiful" rule. Just as one considers the differences of nature and of geography, for appropriate things must be given to all. According to the opinions of the multitude: some live in a sort of calm, while others are unsettled by the winds. Some, with unspeakable numbers of servants, are inclined toward greed. 

Consider also their weaponry:
* A lighter equipment for those who dwell in the mountains.
* A heavier equipment for those living in the hollows <note>valleys or lowlands</note>.

Through their goodwill, even those who have stumbled may be restored. If a city is not of this kind, no one could truly become its legislator. One must choose a political life that is both theoretical and practical. Thus, one must first guard the city in which one dwells as a fatherland. There must be a **concord** <note>original: "homonoia," a state of being of one mind</note> that is in harmony. Even if there are plots or those who have been cast out, the political life must endure despite these oppositions.

<margin>+</margin> We are able, and I appear therefore in this state, being persuaded by nature to handle these matters, which are from the beginning. Spiritual matters are wrought by nature <note>or "nature-crafted"</note> in the Solomonic fashion. We rejoice in her laws. We await the things that follow. 1.

# On the Mastery of Oneself and Others

Concerning the mastery of oneself and one's relations with others. The bodily aspects [of the soul] are governed by the **rational** faculties. For this [virtue] arises when the irrational part of the soul is kept in check. **Courage** <note>original: "andreia"</note> and **temperance** <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note> exist when the flow of the passions is stored up and balanced within their proper part. Define the **spirited** faculty <note>original: "thymetikon" - the seat of anger and drive</note> in this way: it is a component of temperance. For it is a composite of the **rational** <note>original: "logistikon"</note> and the **spirited**, acting as a vehicle that carries and elevates the light [of the soul].

The rational measure is therefore crafted through **prudence** <note>original: "phronesis" - practical wisdom</note>. There is also a rule for the spirited faculty. He says, then, that temperance is spirited; or rather, it is rational, being itself a thing taught by the gods and a standard. And being the temperance of the body, it is firm in those who, through their reflections, exercise their desires and impulses toward the **governing principle** <note>the "hegemonikon" or commanding part of the mind</note>. For courage belongs to the rational faculty. Because no sound is made when temperance is imposed and keeps silent against the <unclear>disturbances</unclear> of fortune. Against these, the desires hold fast for six years <note>likely a reference to a period of Pythagorean or philosophical training</note> alongside speed and diligence.

But in relation to philosophy, [temperance] belongs to the body. **Courage**, on the other hand, is like a **lawful wisdom** <term>lawful wisdom: "ennomos sophia" - wisdom that operates according to the natural laws of the soul</term>. For it does not concern tactical maneuvers; rather, these are stable powers, like a lawful passion. **Justice** <note>original: "dikaiosyne"</note> is a certain harmony and agreement with one another. It is a listening together and a mutual confession, agreeing with one another in the rejection of [false] honors, and it experiences things in such a way as to consider them its own. And this is the body of all **virtue** <note>original: "arete"</note>, just as it is the complete fourfold square of the virtues: **prudence, courage, and temperance.**

The **rational faculty** holds the rule. And [the other parts] hold the second place, so that every virtue may be led by it. For the definition of stable and lawful things belongs to those who possess them, for it is not a matter of hearing alone. What does the lawgiver provide? It is **right reason**. For whatever things happen according to reason and prudence are a "body." And prudence, especially, supports courage. For all things are taught; for they do not see all good things as being in harmony, except through the power of friendship. And this is according to the proportion of that power. For every instance of temperance exists especially through proportion. And generally, every...

Your hand utterly destroyed the nations, and You planted them; You afflicted the peoples and cast them out.
